## Definition

For type S use a fixed sufficiently regular compactly supported orthonormal multiresolution wavelet basis $(\psi_{lk})$ on $[0,1]$ as in [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]], with boundary correction, regularity greater than the truth smoothness $\alpha$, and $|K_l|=2^l$. The spaces $V_L$ spanned by the retained levels $l\le L$ contain constants and have orthonormal scaling bases with uniformly bounded overlap, support diameters at most $C2^{-L}$, and suprema at most $C2^{L/2}$; a fixed shift of the scaling-resolution index is absorbed in $C$. The wavelets likewise have uniformly bounded overlap, support diameters at most $C2^{-l}$, and suprema at most $C2^{l/2}$. For an integer $m>\alpha$, the detail wavelets have vanishing moments through degree $m-1$, and derivatives through order $m$ satisfy $\|\psi_{lk}^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_q2^{l(q+1/2)}$, with uniformly bounded overlap of their supports; the fixed low scaling functions are $C^m$. These are the sufficiently regular compact multiresolution basis conditions in the source density theorem. For the density-model source results, every truth $f_0$ is a probability density satisfying $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$ for constants $\rho_0,D_0$. For $n\ge3$ and smoothness index $\alpha>0$, let $j_n$ and $\ell_n$ be the largest integers satisfying
$$2^{j_n}\le n^{1/(2\alpha+1)},\qquad 2^{\ell_n}\le(n/\log n)^{1/(2\alpha+1)}.$$
Choose one cutoff sequence $L_n\in\{j_n,\ell_n\}$ for all $n\ge3$; set any finite $L_n$ for $n=1,2$, which does not change asymptotic claims.

For a finite wavelet series $T_n=\sum_{l\le L_n}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l\xi_{lk}\psi_{lk}$, define $c(T_n)=\log\int_0^1e^{T_n(x)}dx$ and the normalized log-density $f_n(x)=e^{T_n(x)-c(T_n)}$.

The **type-S1 family** takes IID coefficients $\xi_{lk}$ with a continuous density $\varphi_H$ for which $\log\varphi_H$ is Lipschitz, and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$. Its source theorem assumes $\log f_0$ has coefficient Hölder regularity $\alpha>1$ and $f_0$ is bounded above and bounded away from zero.

The **type-S2 family** takes IID standard-normal coefficients and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(r+1/2)}$, where $0<r<\alpha-1/4$; its source theorem uses $\log f_0\in C^\alpha$, $\alpha>1/2$, and positive finite density bounds.

For the **type-H family**, use the Haar basis instead of the regular type-S wavelets: its scaling function is $1$ and $\psi_{lk}=2^{l/2}(1_{I_{l+1,2k}}-1_{I_{l+1,2k+1}})$ for $l\ge0$ and $0\le k<2^l$. The histogram space at resolution $L$ consists of the scaling coordinate and detail levels $l<L$; all detail coefficients at $l\ge L$ vanish. Partition $[0,1]$ into dyadic cells $I_{L_n,k}$ of length $2^{-L_n}$, draw $\omega=(\omega_k)_{k<2^{L_n}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(a_{0,L_n},\ldots,a_{2^{L_n}-1,L_n})$, and set $f_n=2^{L_n}\omega_k$ on cell $I_{L_n,k}$. The source assumptions are $c_1 2^{-L_na}\le a_{k,L_n}\le c_2$ for fixed positive $a,c_1,c_2$, and $f_0\in C^\alpha$ for $1/2<\alpha\le1$, together with the common positive finite density bounds above. The posterior asymptotic conclusions for these families are separate results.

Here $C^\alpha_\psi$ denotes the coefficient class with norm $\|g\|_{C^\alpha_\psi}:=\sup_{l,k}2^{l(\alpha+1/2)}|\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle|$. For sufficiently regular standard wavelets this is the usual Hölder scale (with the usual Zygmund interpretation at integer smoothness).

## Definition

Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The same coefficient-space definition applies to the Haar system used for type-H histograms: detail levels $l\ge0$ have $2^l$ coefficients, and the single scaling coefficient is an additional finite coarsest coordinate, included in the norm with weight $1$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

## Statement

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a compactly supported wavelet basis of [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The Haar basis with its finite scaling coordinate, as specified in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], is also allowed. Assume each level-$l$ wavelet for $l\ge l_0$ has zero integral, uniformly bounded overlap, support length at most $C_0 2^{-l}$, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. Let $M_0(w)$ be as in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and suppose
$$S_w:=\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}<\infty.$$
For $x\in M_0(w)$ define
$$Jx(t):=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle 1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle_{L^2},\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$
Then this series converges absolutely and uniformly in $t$, $Jx\in C([0,1])$, and $\|Jx-Jy\|_\infty\le C S_w\|x-y\|_{M(w)}$ after adding the finite coarsest-level constant to $C S_w$. If $x$ is the coefficient sequence of $f\in L^2$, then $Jx(t)=\int_0^t f(u)\,du$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The wavelet geometry, summability condition, and multiscale space in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]]: $\|x\|_{M(w)}=\sup_l w_l^{-1}\max_k|x_{lk}|$.

[F2] [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]: $(\psi_{lk})$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2([0,1])$; finite orthogonal projections converge in $L^2$.

## Proof




1.1 For fixed $t$ and level $l\ge l_0$, a wavelet whose support lies wholly on one side of $t$ contributes zero: it is either disjoint from $[0,t]$ or its entire support is integrated and its mean is zero. Only supports meeting $t$ can contribute. Uniformly bounded overlap bounds their number by a constant, and each coefficient has magnitude at most $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. Thus $\sup_t\sum_k|\langle1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle|\le C_1 2^{-l/2}$. The finitely many coarsest levels have a finite uniform sum as well. [given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1] and step 1.1, the absolute sum of all terms at levels $l\ge l_0$ is at most $C_1\|x\|_{M(w)}\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}$, uniformly over $t$. Its tails tend uniformly to zero because $S_w<\infty$. Each finite-level sum is continuous in $t$, since $t\mapsto\int_0^t\psi_{lk}(u)du$ is continuous for an $L^1$ function. The uniform limit is continuous. Applying the same estimate to $x-y$ proves the stated operator-norm bound. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $x_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$ for $f\in L^2$, the finite orthogonal projections converge to $f$ in $L^2$ by [F2]. The map $f\mapsto\int_0^t f(u)du=\langle f,1_{[0,t]}\rangle$ is a continuous $L^2$ functional because $\|1_{[0,t]}\|_2\le1$. Applying it to the finite projections shows that their coefficient sums converge to $\int_0^t f$, while step 2.1 identifies the same limit with $Jx(t)$. [F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

## Example

The uniform truth $f_0=1$ meets the truth-side smoothness and positive-bound conditions for both a type-S log-density prior and a type-H dyadic histogram prior. The weight sequence $w_l=\max(1,\sqrt l\log(l+1))$ is admissible and also satisfies the extra summability needed for the CDF map. Thus the source-specific posterior BvM and credible-band conclusions of [[cor-type-s-h-density-credible-band-calibration]] apply to these choices.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The type-S/type-H definitions of [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]] and the admissible multiscale space of [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]].

[F1] [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]]: both families require a density bounded above and bounded away from zero; type S1 requires $\log f_0\in C^\alpha_\psi$ with $\alpha>1$, type S2 uses $\alpha>1/2$ and $0<r<\alpha-1/4$, while type H requires $f_0\in C^\alpha_\psi$ for $1/2<\alpha\le1$ and the displayed Dirichlet-parameter bounds.

[F2] [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]]: admissibility means $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$.

[F3] [[cor-type-s-h-density-credible-band-calibration]]: the specified prior regimes, truth bounds and admissible summable weights imply posterior weak BvM and asymptotically exact multiscale and CDF credible-band coverage.

## Verification

**Given:** The prior families and $f_0(x)=1$ on $[0,1]$.

1.1 Since $\log f_0=0$ and $f_0=1$, its wavelet coefficient smoothness norm is finite at every order and it is bounded above and away from zero. For type S1 choose $\alpha=2$ and the Laplace density $\varphi_H(x)=\tfrac12e^{-|x|}$, whose logarithm is Lipschitz; its scales are $2^{-l(2+1/2)}$. For type S2 choose $\alpha=2$ and $r=1$, which satisfies $0<1<2-1/4$. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 For type H choose truth smoothness $\alpha=1$, hyperparameters $a=c_1=c_2=1$, and $a_{k,L}=1$ for every cell. Then $2^{-L}\le a_{k,L}\le1$, and the uniform truth belongs to $C^1_\psi$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The sequence $w_l=\max(1,\sqrt l\log(l+1))$ is nondecreasing, since both entries in the maximum are nondecreasing for $l\ge1$. It satisfies $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. Also $\sum_lw_l2^{-l/2}<\infty$ because the ratio of successive terms $\sqrt l\log(l+1)2^{-l/2}$ tends to $2^{-1/2}<1$. Thus it is admissible and meets the CDF primitive summability condition. Steps 1.1–1.2 verify every regime and truth premise of [F3], so its posterior BvM and credible-band conclusions apply to these examples. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra] ∎

manifest_row.statement: The uniform truth $f_0=1$ meets the truth-side smoothness and positive-bound conditions for both a type-S log-density prior and a type-H dyadic histogram prior. The weight sequence $w_l=\max(1,\sqrt l\log(l+1))$ is admissible and also satisfies the extra summability needed for the CDF map. Thus the source-specific posterior BvM and credible-band conclusions of [[cor-type-s-h-density-credible-band-calibration]] apply to these choices.

references.title: Castillo and Nickl, On the Bernstein–von Mises phenomenon for nonparametric Bayes procedures, §3.2

citations.quote:
For type S use a fixed sufficiently regular compactly supported orthonormal multiresolution wavelet basis $(\psi_{lk})$ on $[0,1]$ as in [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]], with boundary correction, regularity greater than the truth smoothness $\alpha$, and $|K_l|=2^l$. The spaces $V_L$ spanned by the retained levels $l\le L$ contain constants and have orthonormal scaling bases with uniformly bounded overlap, support diameters at most $C2^{-L}$, and suprema at most $C2^{L/2}$; a fixed shift of the scaling-resolution index is absorbed in $C$. The wavelets likewise have uniformly bounded overlap, support diameters at most $C2^{-l}$, and suprema at most $C2^{l/2}$. For an integer $m>\alpha$, the detail wavelets have vanishing moments through degree $m-1$, and derivatives through order $m$ satisfy $\|\psi_{lk}^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_q2^{l(q+1/2)}$, with uniformly bounded overlap of their supports; the fixed low scaling functions are $C^m$. These are the sufficiently regular compact multiresolution basis conditions in the source density theorem. For the density-model source results, every truth $f_0$ is a probability density satisfying $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$ for constants $\rho_0,D_0$. For $n\ge3$ and smoothness index $\alpha>0$, let $j_n$ and $\ell_n$ be the largest integers satisfying
$$2^{j_n}\le n^{1/(2\alpha+1)},\qquad 2^{\ell_n}\le(n/\log n)^{1/(2\alpha+1)}.$$
Choose one cutoff sequence $L_n\in\{j_n,\ell_n\}$ for all $n\ge3$; set any finite $L_n$ for $n=1,2$, which does not change asymptotic claims.

For a finite wavelet series $T_n=\sum_{l\le L_n}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l\xi_{lk}\psi_{lk}$, define $c(T_n)=\log\int_0^1e^{T_n(x)}dx$ and the normalized log-density $f_n(x)=e^{T_n(x)-c(T_n)}$.

The **type-S1 family** takes IID coefficients $\xi_{lk}$ with a continuous density $\varphi_H$ for which $\log\varphi_H$ is Lipschitz, and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$. Its source theorem assumes $\log f_0$ has coefficient Hölder regularity $\alpha>1$ and $f_0$ is bounded above and bounded away from zero.

The **type-S2 family** takes IID standard-normal coefficients and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(r+1/2)}$, where $0<r<\alpha-1/4$; its source theorem uses $\log f_0\in C^\alpha$, $\alpha>1/2$, and positive finite density bounds.

For the **type-H family**, use the Haar basis instead of the regular type-S wavelets: its scaling function is $1$ and $\psi_{lk}=2^{l/2}(1_{I_{l+1,2k}}-1_{I_{l+1,2k+1}})$ for $l\ge0$ and $0\le k<2^l$. The histogram space at resolution $L$ consists of the scaling coordinate and detail levels $l<L$; all detail coefficients at $l\ge L$ vanish. Partition $[0,1]$ into dyadic cells $I_{L_n,k}$ of length $2^{-L_n}$, draw $\omega=(\omega_k)_{k<2^{L_n}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(a_{0,L_n},\ldots,a_{2^{L_n}-1,L_n})$, and set $f_n=2^{L_n}\omega_k$ on cell $I_{L_n,k}$. The source assumptions are $c_1 2^{-L_na}\le a_{k,L_n}\le c_2$ for fixed positive $a,c_1,c_2$, and $f_0\in C^\alpha$ for $1/2<\alpha\le1$, together with the common positive finite density bounds above. The posterior asymptotic conclusions for these families are separate results.

Here $C^\alpha_\psi$ denotes the coefficient class with norm $\|g\|_{C^\alpha_\psi}:=\sup_{l,k}2^{l(\alpha+1/2)}|\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle|$. For sufficiently regular standard wavelets this is the usual Hölder scale (with the usual Zygmund interpretation at integer smoothness).

Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The same coefficient-space definition applies to the Haar system used for type-H histograms: detail levels $l\ge0$ have $2^l$ coefficients, and the single scaling coefficient is an additional finite coarsest coordinate, included in the norm with weight $1$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

Assume AC. Use either Type-S1, Type-S2 or Type-H with all the truth, basis, prior-scale, Dirichlet-parameter and cutoff conditions of [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]]. Let $w_l\ge1$ be nondecreasing, $w_l/\sqrt{l+1}\to\infty$, and $\sum_lw_l2^{-l/2}<\infty$. In Type S take $T_n=P_n(L_n)$, the empirical wavelet projection through level $L_n$. In Type H take the empirical histogram $T_n=h_n$ at mesh $2^{-L_n}$, equivalently the Haar projection with scaling coordinate and details $l<L_n$.

For each $0<\eta<1$, the posterior multiscale and CDF balls of [[thm-cdf-and-multiscale-credible-band-calibration-from-bvm]], at posterior level $1-\eta$ and centered at these $T_n$, have posterior mass at least $1-\eta$ and frequentist coverage tending to $1-\eta$. Their scaled radii converge in probability to the positive finite $1-\eta$ quantiles of the corresponding Gaussian bridge norms. In particular the CDF posterior converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance to the $P_0$-Brownian bridge law.

If additionally the coefficient smoothness and undersmoothing hypotheses of [[thm-multiscale-credible-band-holder-diameter]] hold, its intersection with the stated coefficient smoothness ball has the same limiting coverage and the diameter bound asserted there. No unverified entropy, prior-mass, posterior contraction or quantile-regularity premise is required in this corollary.

derivations.claim: Since $\log f_0=0$ and $f_0=1$, its wavelet coefficient smoothness norm is finite at every order and it is bounded above and away from zero. For type S1 choose $\alpha=2$ and the Laplace density $\varphi_H(x)=\tfrac12e^{-|x|}$, whose logarithm is Lipschitz; its scales are $2^{-l(2+1/2)}$. For type S2 choose $\alpha=2$ and $r=1$, which satisfies $0<1<2-1/4$.
For type H choose truth smoothness $\alpha=1$, hyperparameters $a=c_1=c_2=1$, and $a_{k,L}=1$ for every cell. Then $2^{-L}\le a_{k,L}\le1$, and the uniform truth belongs to $C^1_\psi$.

The sequence $w_l=\max(1,\sqrt l\log(l+1))$ is nondecreasing, since both entries in the maximum are nondecreasing for $l\ge1$. It satisfies $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. Also $\sum_lw_l2^{-l/2}<\infty$ because the ratio of successive terms $\sqrt l\log(l+1)2^{-l/2}$ tends to $2^{-1/2}<1$. Thus it is admissible and meets the CDF primitive summability condition. Steps 1.1–1.2 verify every regime and truth premise of [F3], so its posterior BvM and credible-band conclusions apply to these examples.

## Statement

Assume AC. Use either Type-S1, Type-S2 or Type-H with all the truth, basis, prior-scale, Dirichlet-parameter and cutoff conditions of [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]]. Let $w_l\ge1$ be nondecreasing, $w_l/\sqrt{l+1}\to\infty$, and $\sum_lw_l2^{-l/2}<\infty$. In Type S take $T_n=P_n(L_n)$, the empirical wavelet projection through level $L_n$. In Type H take the empirical histogram $T_n=h_n$ at mesh $2^{-L_n}$, equivalently the Haar projection with scaling coordinate and details $l<L_n$.

For each $0<\eta<1$, the posterior multiscale and CDF balls of [[thm-cdf-and-multiscale-credible-band-calibration-from-bvm]], at posterior level $1-\eta$ and centered at these $T_n$, have posterior mass at least $1-\eta$ and frequentist coverage tending to $1-\eta$. Their scaled radii converge in probability to the positive finite $1-\eta$ quantiles of the corresponding Gaussian bridge norms. In particular the CDF posterior converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance to the $P_0$-Brownian bridge law.

If additionally the coefficient smoothness and undersmoothing hypotheses of [[thm-multiscale-credible-band-holder-diameter]] hold, its intersection with the stated coefficient smoothness ball has the same limiting coverage and the diameter bound asserted there. No unverified entropy, prior-mass, posterior contraction or quantile-regularity premise is required in this corollary.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, one of the three source-specific prior regimes, the specified empirical center, admissible summable weights, and $0<\eta<1$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the following suppliers.

[F1] [[thm-type-s-density-weak-bvm-on-m0w]] and [[thm-type-h-histogram-posterior-weak-bvm-in-m0w]] prove posterior bounded-Lipschitz convergence about the respective empirical projections, to the Borel Gaussian bridge with covariance $P_0[(\psi-P_0\psi)(\psi'-P_0\psi')]$.

[F2] [[lem-compact-wavelet-projection-kernel-and-commutator]] preserves coefficient regularity of $e^g$ at every positive order, including integers. [[thm-projected-empirical-process-clt-in-m0w]] proves the sampling CLT for bounded truths with coefficient smoothness $\gamma>1/2$ and either cutoff regime.

[F3] [[lem-density-bridge-norm-cdfs-are-continuous-and-strict]] proves that both bridge norm CDFs are continuous and strictly increasing on positive arguments and have unique positive finite interior quantiles, under the given positive bounded truth and primitive-map summability conditions.

[F4] [[thm-cdf-and-multiscale-credible-band-calibration-from-bvm]] gives measurable credible balls, CDF pushforward convergence, radius limits and exact asymptotic coverage from posterior BvM, the sampling-center CLT and the stated norm-quantile conditions.

[F5] [[thm-multiscale-credible-band-holder-diameter]] gives the additional smoothness-ball coverage and diameter conclusion under its explicit coefficient smoothness and undersmoothing assumptions.

## Proof

1.1 In Type S, [F1] proves posterior BvM about $T_n=P_n(L_n)$ with the original S1 range $\alpha>1$ and original Gaussian S2 range $\alpha>1/2$, $0<r<\alpha-1/4$. The truth $g_0=\log f_0$ has $\alpha$ coefficient regularity, so [F2] gives that regularity for $f_0=e^{g_0}$ as well. The retained basis has the support, overlap and supremum bounds required by the empirical-process theorem in [F2]. Taking $\gamma=\alpha>1/2$ and the given cutoff therefore proves its sampling-center CLT with the same Gaussian bridge. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 In Type H, [F1] proves posterior BvM about the empirical histogram $h_n$. Haar wavelets have the same support, overlap and supremum bounds. The ordinary $\alpha$-Hölder truth, $1/2<\alpha\le1$, has Haar coefficients bounded by $C2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$: subtract its value at one point of the support in the coefficient integral, use the zero mean, support diameter $2^{-l}$ and $L^1$ norm $2^{-l/2}$. The histogram projection retains details through $J_n=L_n-1$. Both given cutoff regimes remain true with this $J_n$, since multiplying $2^{L_n}$ by $1/2$ changes only their comparison constants. Thus [F2] with $\gamma=\alpha$ gives the sampling CLT about this exact histogram center. The finite scaling coordinate is included and its centered fluctuation is zero. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 In all three cases, positivity and boundedness of $f_0$, admissibility, and the displayed summability verify [F3]. Hence every norm-quantile assumption of [F4] holds at $u=1-\eta$. Steps 1.1–1.2 verify its posterior and sampling premises, with the same coefficient covariance law. Applying [F4] proves all asserted CDF limits, measurable credibility, radius limits and frequentist coverage, for the exact empirical centers and every $0<\eta<1$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, given]

2.2 When the additional hypotheses in the last paragraph of the Statement hold, the multiscale credible ball just obtained is precisely the input to [F5]. Applying that theorem yields its smoothness-intersection coverage and stated diameter rate. These are additional hypotheses only for this diameter conclusion; the coverage and CDF conclusions in step 2.1 required no such extra conditions. [F5, step 2.1, given] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID on $[0,1]$ with density $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$, and suppose $g_0=\log f_0\in C^\alpha$. Use a sufficiently regular compactly supported boundary corrected orthonormal multiresolution wavelet basis satisfying [[lem-compact-wavelet-projection-kernel-and-commutator]], with regularity greater than $\alpha$, and let $V_L$ contain exactly its wavelet levels through $L$, including the fixed low scaling space and constants. Its regularity and vanishing moments satisfy the composition hypotheses in that lemma for some integer $m>\alpha$. Let $L_n$ be either of the two cutoff sequences in [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]], fixed consistently for all $n$.

In Type-S1 take $\alpha>1$, $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, and any coefficient probability density with globally Lipschitz logarithm. In Type-S2 take $\alpha>1/2$, Gaussian coefficients, and $\sigma_l=2^{-l(r+1/2)}$ with $0<r<\alpha-1/4$. Normalize $f=\exp(T)/\int\exp(T)$ as in that definition. For every admissible weight sequence $w$, the posterior satisfies
$$\beta_{BL,M_0(w)}\bigl(\mathcal L(\sqrt n(f-P_n(L_n))\mid X^n),\mathcal L(G_{P_0})\bigr)\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0^n$-probability, where $P_n(L_n)$ has empirical wavelet coefficients through $L_n$ and zero coefficients above $L_n$, and $G_{P_0}$ is the Borel Gaussian bridge with covariance $P_0[(\psi_i-P_0\psi_i)(\psi_j-P_0\psi_j)]$.

Assume AC. Use the type-H prior of [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]], retaining its original conditions: $1/2<\alpha\le1$, $f_0\in C^\alpha([0,1])$, $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$, either original cutoff $L_n=j_n$ or $L_n=\ell_n$, and $c_1 2^{-L_na}\le a_{k,L_n}\le c_2$ for fixed positive $a,c_1,c_2$. Write $m_n=2^{L_n}$. In the Haar convention, the scaling function is $1$, the detail functions are
$$\psi_{lk}=2^{l/2}(\mathbf1_{I_{l+1,2k}}-\mathbf1_{I_{l+1,2k+1}}),\qquad l\ge0,\quad 0\le k<2^l,$$
and a histogram at resolution $L_n$ has only the scaling coordinate and levels $l<L_n$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID from $f_0$, let $N_{nk}=\sum_i\mathbf1_{I_{L_n,k}}(X_i)$, and define the empirical histogram
$$h_n(x)=m_n N_{nk}/n\quad\text{on }I_{L_n,k}.$$
Let $\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X^n)$ be the density posterior for the stated histogram prior. For every nondecreasing $w_l\ge1$ with $w_l/\sqrt{l+1}\to\infty$, its conditional law $Q_n$ of $\sqrt n(f-h_n)$ satisfies
$$\beta_{BL,M_0(w)}(Q_n,\mathcal L(G_{P_0}))\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0^n$-probability, where the Borel centered Gaussian bridge $G_{P_0}$ is supplied by [[lem-density-gaussian-bridge-is-borel-on-m0w]] and has covariance $P_0[(\psi-P_0\psi)(\psi'-P_0\psi')]$. Its scaling coordinate is zero. This proves the type-H source-specific posterior BvM with the empirical projection center; no additional contraction, bias, or Dirichlet-parameter condition is imposed.

Let $V_L$ be the span of wavelets through level $L$ in a compactly supported orthonormal multiresolution basis on $[0,1]$, either boundary corrected or periodized. Assume constants belong to $V_L$, its dimension $d_L\asymp2^L$, and its orthonormal scaling functions $\phi_{Lk}$ have supremum norm at most $C2^{L/2}$, support diameter at most $C2^{-L}$, and uniformly bounded overlap. Periodized supports and distances are interpreted on the circle. Assume also $\sum_k|\psi_{lk}(x)|\le C2^{l/2}$ and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C2^{-l/2}$. Let $P_L$ denote the orthogonal projection onto $V_L$.

Then $P_L$ has a kernel $K_L$ satisfying $\sup_x\int|K_L(x,y)|dy\le C'$ and $K_L(x,y)=0$ when $\operatorname{dist}(x,y)>C'2^{-L}$. If $a$ is $\beta$-Hölder for $0<\beta\le1$, then
$$\|P_L(ah)-ah\|_\infty\le C'\|a\|_{C^\beta}2^{-\beta L}\|h\|_\infty,\qquad h\in V_L.$$
For the composition assertion, assume additionally an integer $m>\alpha$ such that $\|\psi_{lk}^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_q2^{l(q+1/2)}$ for $0\le q\le m$, bounded overlap also for their derivatives, and vanishing moments through degree $m-1$ for the detail wavelets, including boundary wavelets; the finite low scaling functions are $C^m$. These are the usual sufficiently regular compact wavelet hypotheses. If a bounded function $g$ has coefficients bounded by $C_g2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, with $\alpha>0$, and its wavelet expansion represents $g$ in $L^2$, then $\|g-P_Lg\|_\infty\le C''C_g2^{-\alpha L}$, up to equality of the continuous representatives. Under these additional derivative and cancellation hypotheses, $e^g$ also has coefficients bounded by $C_g^\prime2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, including integer $\alpha$, and $g,e^g$ are $\beta$-Hölder for every $0<\beta<\min(\alpha,1)$. Moreover $\|h\|_\infty\le C''\sqrt{d_L}\|h\|_2$ for $h\in V_L$.

Assume AC. Let $P_0$ have a density $f_0$ on $[0,1]$ with $\|f_0\|_\infty\le B<\infty$. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be an orthonormal, compactly supported wavelet basis with $2^l$ coefficients at level $l\ge1$, uniformly bounded overlap, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_\infty\le C_0 2^{l/2}$. Suppose for some $\gamma>1/2$,
$$\max_k|\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle|\le C_f2^{-l(\gamma+1/2)}.$$
Let $w_l\ge1$ be nondecreasing and admissible in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and choose either cutoff regime
$$2^{L_n}\asymp n^{1/(2\gamma+1)}\quad\text{or}\quad 2^{L_n}\asymp(n/\log n)^{1/(2\gamma+1)}.$$
For IID $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, define the finite wavelet projection $P_n(L_n)$ by coefficients $\langle P_n(L_n),\psi_{lk}\rangle=P_n\psi_{lk}:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_{lk}(X_i)$ for $l\le L_n$ and zero for $l>L_n$, with the coarsest scaling coordinates projected as well. Let $G_{P_0}$ be a Borel centered Gaussian law on $M_0(w)$ whose coefficient covariance is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(G_{lk},G_{l'k'})=P_0[(\psi_{lk}-P_0\psi_{lk})(\psi_{l'k'}-P_0\psi_{l'k'})].$$
Then
$$\sqrt n\{P_n(L_n)-f_0\}\Rightarrow G_{P_0}\quad\text{in }M_0(w).$$

Assume AC. Let $P_0$ have density $0<\rho\le f_0\le D<\infty$ on $[0,1]$, and put $F_0(t)=\int_0^t f_0$. Use a complete real orthonormal wavelet basis, allowing the Haar basis with its finite scaling coordinate, and admissible weights $w$ as in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]]. Assume the wavelet geometry and summability conditions of [[lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs]], and write $J:M_0(w)\to C([0,1])$ for its primitive map. Let $G$ be the Borel centered Gaussian bridge random element of [[lem-density-gaussian-bridge-is-borel-on-m0w]], with coefficient covariance
$$\operatorname{Cov}(G_{lk},G_{l'k'})=P_0[(\psi_{lk}-P_0\psi_{lk})(\psi_{l'k'}-P_0\psi_{l'k'})].$$
Then the distribution functions of $\|G\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|JG\|_\infty$ are continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$. Both assign probability zero to $0$, and take values strictly between $0$ and $1$ at every positive argument. Consequently, for every $u\in(0,1)$, each has a unique positive finite lower $u$-quantile $q$, with CDF value $u$, and is strictly increasing on an open neighborhood of $q$.

Let $P_0$ have a density $f_0$ on $[0,1]$ bounded above and bounded away from zero, and put $F_0(t)=\int_0^t f_0(x)dx$. Use the wavelet basis and $M_0(w)$ of [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and assume the wavelet conditions and summability condition $\sum_lw_l2^{-l/2}<\infty$ of [[lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs]]. Let $T_n$ be a measurable $L^2$-valued center, let $\Pi_n$ be a posterior kernel supported on $L^2$ densities, and define $Q_n$ to be the conditional law on $M_0(w)$ of $\sqrt n(f-T_n)$ under $f\sim\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X^n)$.

Assume under $P_0^n$ that (i) $Q_n$ converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance in probability to the centered Gaussian bridge coefficient law $G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$, whose finite coefficient covariances are $P_0[(h-P_0h)(g-P_0g)]$, and (ii) $\sqrt n(T_n-f_0)\Rightarrow G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$. For $u=1-\alpha$, let $q_M$ and $q_C$ be the lower $u$-quantiles of $\|G_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|JG_{P_0}\|_\infty$. Assume both CDFs are continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on open neighborhoods of their respective quantiles, and that $q_M,q_C>0$. These local quantile conditions allow the CDFs to be constant on the negative half-line. In the projected empirical-center case $T_n=P_n(L_n)$, [[thm-projected-empirical-process-clt-in-m0w]] supplies premise (ii) under its stated smoothness and cutoff conditions. For the source-specific type-S and type-H priors, the posterior BvM premise (i) is established in [[thm-type-s-density-weak-bvm-on-m0w]] and [[thm-type-h-histogram-posterior-weak-bvm-in-m0w]], respectively.

For a posterior draw $f$, write $F_f=Jf$ and $F_{T_n}=JT_n$, where $J$ is the primitive map of [[lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs]]. Then the posterior law of $\sqrt n(F_f-F_{T_n})$ converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance on $C([0,1])$ to the $P_0$-Brownian bridge $B_{P_0}(t)$, with covariance $F_0(s\wedge t)-F_0(s)F_0(t)$.

For $0<\alpha<1$, let $R_n^M$ and $R_n^C$ be the posterior lower $1-\alpha$ quantiles of $\|\sqrt n(f-T_n)\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|\sqrt n(F_f-F_{T_n})\|_\infty$, respectively. The corresponding posterior balls
$$C_n^M=\{f:\|f-T_n\|_{M(w)}\le R_n^M/\sqrt n\},\qquad C_n^C=\{F:\|F-F_{T_n}\|_\infty\le R_n^C/\sqrt n\}$$
are measurable credible sets of posterior mass at least $1-\alpha$. Their frequentist coverage tends to $1-\alpha$, and the scaled radii converge to the respective $1-\alpha$ quantiles of $\|G_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|B_{P_0}\|_\infty$.

Use the $M_0(w)$ credible ball $C_n^M$ and radius $R_n^M$ of [[thm-cdf-and-multiscale-credible-band-calibration-from-bvm]]. Let $\gamma>0$, assume the compactly supported wavelets have uniformly bounded overlap and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_\infty\le C2^{l/2}$, and define
$$\|f\|_{C^\gamma_\psi}:=\sup_{l,k}2^{l(\gamma+1/2)}|\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle|.$$
Suppose $\|f_0\|_{C^\gamma_\psi}<\infty$. Choose integers $j_n$ with $2^{j_n}\asymp(n/\log n)^{1/(2\gamma+1)}$ and let $u_n=w_{j_n}/\sqrt{j_n}\to\infty$. Intersect the credible ball with the coefficient smoothness ball:
$$\overline C_n=C_n^M\cap\{f:\|f\|_{C^\gamma_\psi}\le u_n\}.$$
Then $P_{f_0}^{(n)}\{f_0\in\overline C_n\}\to1-\alpha$, and its $L^\infty$ diameter satisfies
$$\operatorname{diam}_{L^\infty}(\overline C_n)=O_{P_{f_0}^{(n)}}\!\left((n/\log n)^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+1)}u_n\right).$$

derivations.claim: In Type S, [F1] proves posterior BvM about $T_n=P_n(L_n)$ with the original S1 range $\alpha>1$ and original Gaussian S2 range $\alpha>1/2$, $0<r<\alpha-1/4$. The truth $g_0=\log f_0$ has $\alpha$ coefficient regularity, so [F2] gives that regularity for $f_0=e^{g_0}$ as well. The retained basis has the support, overlap and supremum bounds required by the empirical-process theorem in [F2]. Taking $\gamma=\alpha>1/2$ and the given cutoff therefore proves its sampling-center CLT with the same Gaussian bridge.

In Type H, [F1] proves posterior BvM about the empirical histogram $h_n$. Haar wavelets have the same support, overlap and supremum bounds. The ordinary $\alpha$-Hölder truth, $1/2<\alpha\le1$, has Haar coefficients bounded by $C2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$: subtract its value at one point of the support in the coefficient integral, use the zero mean, support diameter $2^{-l}$ and $L^1$ norm $2^{-l/2}$. The histogram projection retains details through $J_n=L_n-1$. Both given cutoff regimes remain true with this $J_n$, since multiplying $2^{L_n}$ by $1/2$ changes only their comparison constants. Thus [F2] with $\gamma=\alpha$ gives the sampling CLT about this exact histogram center. The finite scaling coordinate is included and its centered fluctuation is zero.

In all three cases, positivity and boundedness of $f_0$, admissibility, and the displayed summability verify [F3]. Hence every norm-quantile assumption of [F4] holds at $u=1-\eta$. Steps 1.1–1.2 verify its posterior and sampling premises, with the same coefficient covariance law. Applying [F4] proves all asserted CDF limits, measurable credibility, radius limits and frequentist coverage, for the exact empirical centers and every $0<\eta<1$.

When the additional hypotheses in the last paragraph of the Statement hold, the multiscale credible ball just obtained is precisely the input to [F5]. Applying that theorem yields its smoothness-intersection coverage and stated diameter rate. These are additional hypotheses only for this diameter conclusion; the coverage and CDF conclusions in step 2.1 required no such extra conditions.

proof_contract.claim:
Assume AC. Use either Type-S1, Type-S2 or Type-H with all the truth, basis, prior-scale, Dirichlet-parameter and cutoff conditions of [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]]. Let $w_l\ge1$ be nondecreasing, $w_l/\sqrt{l+1}\to\infty$, and $\sum_lw_l2^{-l/2}<\infty$. In Type S take $T_n=P_n(L_n)$, the empirical wavelet projection through level $L_n$. In Type H take the empirical histogram $T_n=h_n$ at mesh $2^{-L_n}$, equivalently the Haar projection with scaling coordinate and details $l<L_n$.

For each $0<\eta<1$, the posterior multiscale and CDF balls of [[thm-cdf-and-multiscale-credible-band-calibration-from-bvm]], at posterior level $1-\eta$ and centered at these $T_n$, have posterior mass at least $1-\eta$ and frequentist coverage tending to $1-\eta$. Their scaled radii converge in probability to the positive finite $1-\eta$ quantiles of the corresponding Gaussian bridge norms. In particular the CDF posterior converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance to the $P_0$-Brownian bridge law.

If additionally the coefficient smoothness and undersmoothing hypotheses of [[thm-multiscale-credible-band-holder-diameter]] hold, its intersection with the stated coefficient smoothness ball has the same limiting coverage and the diameter bound asserted there. No unverified entropy, prior-mass, posterior contraction or quantile-regularity premise is required in this corollary.

lem-density-normal-laws-and-square-summa.claim:
Assume countable choice. Put $g(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Then $\gamma(E)=\int_Eg(x)\,dx$ is a Borel probability on $\mathbb R$. In this item and its applications, write $N(m,v)$ for its pushforward under $x\mapsto m+\sqrt v\,x$, where $v\ge0$; thus $N(m,0)=\delta_m$. This density convention requires no full axiom of choice. For $v>0$ the law has density
$$g_{m,v}(x)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}\exp\{- (x-m)^2/(2v)\},$$
and its CDF is continuous and strictly increasing. Its mean and variance are $m$ and $v$.

If $Z_j$ are mutually independent with density $g$ and $\sum_{j\ge1}c_j^2=v<\infty$, and the finite sums $S_m=\sum_{j\le m}c_jZ_j$ converge in probability to a supplied real random variable $S$, then $S$ has law $N(0,v)$. In particular, this applies whenever the sums converge almost surely or in $L^2$.

citations.quote: $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ ([[def-derivative]]), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.**
With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim: The positive continuous function $g$ is Borel measurable, since inverse images of open sets are open. For an integer $R\ge1$, substitute $x=\sqrt2\,t$ in the continuous compact-interval integral. The bridge in [F1] and then increasing truncation in [F2] give $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=\sqrt2\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{-R/\sqrt2}^{R/\sqrt2}e^{-t^2}\,dt=\sqrt{2\pi}$. Thus [F2] makes $\gamma$ a probability. For $v>0$, compact substitutions in the same way show that its affine pushforward has the asserted half-line integrals of $g_{m,v}$; limits of compact intervals give the half-lines, and [F5] gives equality of the measures. For $v=0$ the affine map is constant, giving the Dirac law directly.

The CDF of $N(m,v)$ for $v>0$ is continuous, since $g_{m,v}$ is bounded and the integral over an interval of length $h$ is at most $|h|/\sqrt{2\pi v}$. It is strictly increasing because the positive continuous density has a positive minimum on every nondegenerate compact interval. For $Z$ with density $g$, $g'(x)=-xg(x)$, and integration by parts gives $\int_{-R}^R|x|g(x)dx=2(g(0)-g(R))$ and $\int_{-R}^Rx^2g(x)dx=\int_{-R}^Rg(x)dx-2Rg(R)$. The exponential series shows $g(R)\to0$ and $Rg(R)\to0$. Increasing truncation gives $\mathbb E|Z|<\infty$ and $\mathbb EZ^2=1$; symmetry gives $\mathbb EZ=0$. Expanding $m+\sqrt v Z$ gives the claimed mean and variance, also for $v=0$.

Let $U,V$ be independent centered density normal variables with variances $a,b>0$. Their sum has density $h(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}g_{0,a}(u)g_{0,b}(x-u)du$. Indeed, [F4] expresses $P(U+V\le x)$ as the nonnegative double integral of $\mathbf1_{u+t\le x}g_{0,a}(u)g_{0,b}(t)$; for each fixed $u$, a translation in the continuous half-line integral followed by Tonelli gives $\int_{-\infty}^xh(y)dy$. These half-line probabilities determine the law by [F5]. Completing the square gives
$$\frac{u^2}{a}+\frac{(x-u)^2}{b}=\frac{a+b}{ab}\left(u-\frac{ax}{a+b}\right)^2+\frac{x^2}{a+b}.$$
The compact substitutions and increasing limits in step 1.1 therefore give $h(x)=g_{0,a+b}(x)$. If either variance is zero the corresponding variable is zero almost surely and the same conclusion is immediate. Scaling a coordinate by a negative coefficient gives the same density as scaling by its absolute value, by the symmetry of $g$. Finite induction, using mutual independence to separate the last coordinate from the preceding tuple, proves $S_m\sim N(0,v_m)$ with $v_m=\sum_{j\le m}c_j^2$.

If $v=0$, every coefficient is zero, so convergence in probability implies $S=0$ almost surely. Suppose $v>0$. Then $v_m\to v$ and eventually $v_m>0$. Write $\Phi$ for the continuous CDF of $\gamma$. For any $x\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$, convergence in probability and step 2.1 give
$$\Phi((x-\varepsilon)/\sqrt{v_m})-P(|S_m-S|>\varepsilon)\le P(S\le x)\le\Phi((x+\varepsilon)/\sqrt{v_m})+P(|S_m-S|>\varepsilon).$$
First let $m\to\infty$, then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Continuity from step 1.2 gives $P(S\le x)=\Phi(x/\sqrt v)$ for every $x$. By [F5], $S$ has law $N(0,v)$. Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability by dominated convergence on the indicators of $\{|S_m-S|>\varepsilon\}$, and $L^2$ convergence implies it by $\varepsilon^2P(|S_m-S|>\varepsilon)\le\mathbb E|S_m-S|^2$.

boundaries.reason: The series is indexed by the supplied positive integers; there is no free empty family. Zero finite sums and vanishing coefficients are covered by the zero-variance branch.

lem-white-noise-is-borel-gaussian-on-neg.claim: Assume countable choice. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be the wavelet or trigonometric basis from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. Let $Z_{lk}$ be mutually independent real random variables with density $g(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Define the formal white-noise coefficient sequence $W=(Z_{lk})$. For every $\delta>1/2$, this sequence is almost surely an element of $H(\delta)$ and is a Borel Gaussian random element there. Its law $N$ is a Borel probability on $H(\delta)$. For an infinite-dimensional basis, white noise is not an $L^2([0,1])$-valued random element. Here Gaussian means that each continuous real linear functional has a centered law $N(0,v)$ in the density convention of [[lem-density-normal-laws-and-square-summable-gaussian-series]]; in particular, for $L(c)=\sum_jd_jc_j$ its variance is $\sum_jd_j^2$ whenever this pairing is continuous on $H(\delta)$.

citations.quote:
Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Assume countable choice. Put $g(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Then $\gamma(E)=\int_Eg(x)\,dx$ is a Borel probability on $\mathbb R$. In this item and its applications, write $N(m,v)$ for its pushforward under $x\mapsto m+\sqrt v\,x$, where $v\ge0$; thus $N(m,0)=\delta_m$. This density convention requires no full axiom of choice. For $v>0$ the law has density
$$g_{m,v}(x)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}\exp\{- (x-m)^2/(2v)\},$$
and its CDF is continuous and strictly increasing. Its mean and variance are $m$ and $v$.

If $Z_j$ are mutually independent with density $g$ and $\sum_{j\ge1}c_j^2=v<\infty$, and the finite sums $S_m=\sum_{j\le m}c_jZ_j$ converge in probability to a supplied real random variable $S$, then $S$ has law $N(0,v)$. In particular, this applies whenever the sums converge almost surely or in $L^2$.

derivations.claim: Write $w_l=a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$. In the wavelet case, the trace sum is a finite coarsest term plus $\sum_{l\ge1}2^lw_l=(\log2)^{-2\delta}\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$. On each block $2^m\le l<2^{m+1}$, the sum of $l^{-r}$ is between $2^m2^{-r(m+1)}$ and $2^m2^{-rm}$; hence these blocks form a convergent geometric series when $r>1$, while for $r\le1$ their contributions are bounded below by a fixed positive constant and the series diverges. For trigonometric coefficients with bounded multiplicities, the block $2^m\le |l|<2^{m+1}$ contributes between constant multiples of $m^{-2\delta}$ to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The same comparison therefore gives finiteness exactly when $\delta>1/2$. Thus the trace $T_\delta:=\sum_{l,k}w_l$ is finite in either case.

Let $S_m$ be the sum of $w_lZ_{lk}^2$ over the first $m$ coordinates in the fixed countable enumeration. These nonnegative partial sums increase to $S=\sum_{l,k}w_lZ_{lk}^2$, and [F3] gives $\mathbb ES=\lim_m\mathbb ES_m=\sum_{l,k}w_l=T_\delta$. The mean and second moment of each coordinate are $0$ and $1$ by [F5]. If $S=\infty$ on a set of probability $p>0$, then $\mathbb ES\ge Rp$ for every $R>0$, impossible; hence $S<\infty$ almost surely.

On that probability-one event, the finite-coordinate sums of $W$ are Cauchy in $H(\delta)$ because the squared norm of every tail is the corresponding tail of the convergent series $S$. Completeness gives a limit in $H(\delta)$. The Cauchy event is measurable, and the partial sums are measurable; their pointwise limit on that event is measurable as an $H(\delta)$-valued map because the space is separable. Setting it to zero on the measurable complement gives a Borel random element.

Let $e_j$ be the unit vector of the weighted sequence Hilbert space supported on coordinate $j$ and let $b_j=L(e_j)$ for a continuous real linear functional $L$. For each finite set $F$, boundedness applied to $\sum_{j\in F}b_je_j$ gives $\sum_{j\in F}b_j^2\le\|L\|^2$, so $\sum_jb_j^2<\infty$. Since the weights $w_j$ are bounded, $v:=\sum_jw_jb_j^2<\infty$. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

$$f_N=\sum_{0\le l\le N}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l\xi_{lk}\psi_{lk}.$$

Assume countable choice, denoted $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, when specializing to $H=L^2([0,1])$. Then $f_N$ converges almost surely in $H$ to a Borel $H$-valued random element $f$, and

Assume countable choice. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be the wavelet or trigonometric basis from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. Let $Z_{lk}$ be mutually independent real random variables with density $g(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Define the formal white-noise coefficient sequence $W=(Z_{lk})$. For every $\delta>1/2$, this sequence is almost surely an element of $H(\delta)$ and is a Borel Gaussian random element there. Its law $N$ is a Borel probability on $H(\delta)$. For an infinite-dimensional basis, white noise is not an $L^2([0,1])$-valued random element. Here Gaussian means that each continuous real linear functional has a centered law $N(0,v)$ in the density convention of [[lem-density-normal-laws-and-square-summable-gaussian-series]]; in particular, for $L(c)=\sum_jd_jc_j$ its variance is $\sum_jd_j^2$ whenever this pairing is continuous on $H(\delta)$.

Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex inner-product
space $H$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).
Then for every $x\in H$ the nonnegative family
$\bigl(|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2\bigr)_{i\in I}$ has finite sum in the
finite-subset-supremum convention
([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]) and

$$\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2\le\|x\|^2 .$$

In particular the coefficient family $(\langle x,e_i\rangle)_{i\in I}$ belongs

derivations.claim: Enumerate the wavelet coefficients as $j=1,2,\ldots$ and let $P_m$ retain the first $m$ coordinates. The sigma-algebra generated by all coordinate maps is the Borel sigma-algebra of $H(\delta)$. Indeed, the coordinate maps are continuous, so their sigma-algebra is contained in the Borel sigma-algebra. Conversely, for any closed set $C\subseteq H(\delta)$, $x\mapsto d(P_mx,C)$ is measurable with respect to the coordinate sigma-algebra and converges to $d(x,C)$ by [F1]. Thus $C=\{x:d(x,C)=0\}$ belongs to that sigma-algebra.

Write $p_j(x)=(n/2\pi)^{1/2}e^{-n(x-\theta_{0,j})^2/2}$ for the true coordinate density. The prior-predictive coordinate density is
$$q_j(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}(n/2\pi)^{1/2}e^{-n(x-t)^2/2}\,\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(t/\sigma_j)\,dt,$$
where $\sigma_j=\sigma_l$ for $j=(l,k)$. Both densities are positive and integrate to one. Put $h_j^2=\int(\sqrt{p_j}-\sqrt{q_j})^2dx$ and $\rho_j=\int\sqrt{p_jq_j}\,dx=1-h_j^2/2$. Since square root is concave, the affinity with a mixture is at least the mixture of the affinities. The affinity of two normal densities with variance $1/n$ and means $a,b$ is $e^{-n(a-b)^2/8}$. Therefore
$$h_j^2\le\int 2\bigl(1-e^{-n(t-\theta_{0,j})^2/8}\bigr)\,\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(t/\sigma_j)dt\le\frac n4\int(t-\theta_{0,j})^2\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(t/\sigma_j)dt\le\frac n2(\theta_{0,j}^2+\sigma_j^2m_2).$$
By [F2] and [F3] the prior-predictive and true coordinates are each independent across $j$. By [F4] and the geometric-series formula, $\sum_j\theta_{0,j}^2<\infty$ and $\sum_j\sigma_j^2=\sum_{l\ge0}2^{-2\alpha l}<\infty$. Hence $\sum_jh_j^2<\infty$ and $\sum_j(1-\rho_j)<\infty$.

Let $\mathcal F_m$ be the sigma-algebra of the first $m$ coordinates on $H(\delta)$ and set $L_m=\prod_{j\le m}p_j(X_j)/q_j(X_j)$. Under $Q_n$, $L_m$ is the density of the first $m$ true coordinates relative to the first $m$ prior-predictive coordinates, and $\mathbb E_{Q_n}L_m=1$. For $r>m$, independence gives
$$\mathbb E_{Q_n}\!\left[\sqrt{L_rL_m}\right]=\prod_{m<j\le r}\rho_j,$$
so $\|\sqrt{L_r}-\sqrt{L_m}\|_{L^2(Q_n)}^2=2\bigl(1-\prod_{m<j\le r}\rho_j\bigr)\le2\sum_{m<j\le r}(1-\rho_j)\to0$ uniformly in $r>m$. Thus $\sqrt{L_m}$ is Cauchy in $L^2(Q_n)$. Also
$$\|L_r-L_m\|_{L^1(Q_n)}\le\|\sqrt{L_r}-\sqrt{L_m}\|_2\,\|\sqrt{L_r}+\sqrt{L_m}\|_2\le2\|\sqrt{L_r}-\sqrt{L_m}\|_2,$$
so $L_m\to L$ in $L^1(Q_n)$ for some nonnegative $L$ with $\int L\,dQ_n=1$.

For every event $A\in\mathcal F_m$ and $r\ge m$, the finite-coordinate density identity and independence of the remaining coordinates give $\int_A L_r\,dQ_n=P_{f_0}^{(n)}(A)$. Passing to the $L^1$ limit gives $\int_A L\,dQ_n=P_{f_0}^{(n)}(A)$. Such finite-coordinate cylinder events form a generating pi-system by step 1.1; [F5] therefore gives $P_{f_0}^{(n)}(A)=\int_A L\,dQ_n$ for every Borel $A\subseteq H(\delta)$. Thus $P_{f_0}^{(n)}\ll Q_n$. Interchanging $p_j$ and $q_j$ gives the same argument and proves $Q_n\ll P_{f_0}^{(n)}$.

thm-weak-nonparametric-bernstein-von-mis.claim:
Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be the S-regular wavelet basis in [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]], with $2^l$ coefficients at each level $l\ge0$. For $\alpha>0$, put $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$ and let the prior on $f=\sum_{l,k}\sigma_l\xi_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ have IID coefficients $\xi_{lk}$ with density $\varphi$. Assume countable choice for the $L^2$ prior construction supplied by [[lem-wavelet-product-prior-is-l2-valued]], and take the full posterior kernel as the supplied model input of [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]]. Let $f_0\in L^2([0,1])$, write $\theta_{0,lk}=\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle$ and $r_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}/\sigma_l$, and suppose

$$\sup_{l,k}|r_{lk}|\le M<\tau,$$

where $\varphi$ is a probability density satisfying $\varphi(u)\le C_\varphi$ for every $u$, $\varphi(u)\ge c_\varphi>0$ for $|u|<\tau$, $\int u^2\varphi(u)\,du<\infty$, and $\varphi$ is continuous at each $r_{lk}$. The observation model is

$$dX^{(n)}(t)=f_0(t)\,dt+n^{-1/2}dW(t),\qquad 0\le t\le1,$$

with standard white noise $W$; in the stated basis this is the sequence experiment $X_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}+n^{-1/2}Z_{lk}$ with independent standard normal coordinates. Let $\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X)$ be the product-coordinate posterior of [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]]. Let $N$ be the law of the canonical white noise in $H(\delta)$ and define

$$\widetilde\Pi_n:=\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X)\circ[f\mapsto\sqrt n(f-X)]^{-1},\qquad \beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(\mu,\nu):=\sup_{\substack{\|g\|_\infty\le1\\ \operatorname{Lip}_{H(\delta)}(g)\le1}}\left|\int g\,d\mu-\int g\,d\nu\right|.$$

For every $\delta>1/2$,

$$\beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(\widetilde\Pi_n,N)\longrightarrow0$$

in probability under the true white-noise law $P_{f_0}^{(n)}$. This is a bounded-Lipschitz weak BvM conclusion; it asserts neither total-variation convergence on all Borel subsets nor an $L^2$-valued Gaussian limit.

Assume countable choice for the $L^2$-valued prior construction. Let the wavelet product prior have independent coefficients $\theta_{lk}=\sigma_l\xi_{lk}$, where the $\xi_{lk}$ are IID with density $\varphi$. Observe the independent Gaussian sequence

there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $\delta>1/2$ and choose $\delta'$ with $1/2<\delta'<\delta$. Let $P_J$ retain all wavelet coordinates with level $l\le J$. Since $w_l^\delta/w_l^{\delta'}=(\log a_l)^{-2(\delta-\delta')}$ and $a_l\to\infty$, for $q_J:=(\log a_{J+1})^{-(\delta-\delta')}$ one has $\|(I-P_J)u\|_{H(\delta)}\le q_J\|u\|_{H(\delta')}\quad\text{and}\quad q_J\to0.$ For any probability law $Q$ on $H(\delta)$, coupling $U$ with $P_JU$ and using the defining Lipschitz bound gives $\beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(Q,Q\circ P_J^{-1})\le\int\|(I-P_J)u\|_{H(\delta)}\,Q(du)$.

For a fixed $J$, the middle term in $\beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(\widetilde\Pi_n,N)\le\beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(\widetilde\Pi_n,\widetilde\Pi_n\circ P_J^{-1})+\beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(\widetilde\Pi_n\circ P_J^{-1},N\circ P_J^{-1})+\beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(N\circ P_J^{-1},N)$ tends to zero in probability: [F5] gives $L^1$ convergence of the projected posterior and Gaussian coordinate densities. Every bounded-Lipschitz test function restricted to the projected subspace is bounded by $1$, so its integral difference is at most that $L^1$ distance.

The last term is bounded by $\mathbb E\|W-P_JW\|_{H(\delta)}$, which is at most $\bigl(\mathbb E\|W-P_JW\|_{H(\delta)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}=\bigl(\sum_{l>J,k}w_l^\delta\bigr)^{1/2}$ by [F3] and [F7]. This tends to zero as $J\to\infty$ by [F1].

Under the joint true-data/posterior law, using the supplied posterior model [F6] and the $L^2$ prior construction [F2], $U=\sqrt n(f-X)=\sqrt n(f-f_0)-W$, where $W=\sqrt n(X-f_0)$ has law $N$. By [F4], [F3] and $(a-b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$, $\mathbb E_{f_0}^{(n)}\int\|U\|_{H(\delta')}^2\,\Pi_n(df\mid X)\le2n\mathbb E_{f_0}^{(n)}\int\|f-f_0\|_{H(\delta')}^2\,\Pi_n(df\mid X)+2\mathbb E\|W\|_{H(\delta')}^2\le C,$ with $C$ independent of $n$. Applying [F7] under the posterior probability and then under the true-data probability, together with step 1.1, gives $\mathbb E_{f_0}^{(n)}\beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(\widetilde\Pi_n,\widetilde\Pi_n\circ P_J^{-1})\le q_J\sqrt C.$ Thus the first projection error can be made uniformly small by taking $J$ large.

Fix $0<\varepsilon<1$ and choose $J$ so the expected first and deterministic third terms are each less than $\varepsilon^2$. By [F8], the probability that the first term exceeds $\varepsilon$ is at most $\varepsilon$; the deterministic third term is less than $\varepsilon$. For this fixed $J$, step 1.2 makes the probability that the middle term exceeds $\varepsilon$ tend to zero. The triangle bound then gives a limiting upper bound $\varepsilon$ for the probability that the full distance exceeds $3\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, $\beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(\widetilde\Pi_n,N)\to0$ in $P_{f_0}^{(n)}$-probability.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix $\delta>1/2$. For every bounded $1$-Lipschitz function $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, the composition $h\circ L_g$ is bounded by $1$ and has Lipschitz constant at most $\|L_g\|_{H(\delta)^*}$. Rescaling by $c_g=\max(1,\|L_g\|_{H(\delta)^*})$ makes it an admissible bounded-Lipschitz test on $H(\delta)$. Hence the scalar pushforward distance is at most $c_g$ times the distance in [F1]. The pushforward of $N$ is $N(0,\sigma_g^2)$ by [F3], proving the asserted scalar BvM limit.

Translate the posterior law of $L_g(f)$ by $L_g(X^{(n)})$ and scale by $\sqrt n$. By [F4] and the continuous strictly increasing normal CDF from [F6], the two quantiles of this scaled law converge in probability to $\sigma_g z_{\alpha/2}$ and $\sigma_g z_{1-\alpha/2}$, where $z_u$ is the $u$-quantile of $N(0,1)$. Since the affine map is increasing, these are exactly the scaled endpoints of $C_{n,\alpha}-L_g(X^{(n)})$. The interval is credible by [F5].

Under the true white-noise law, $\sqrt n\{L_g(X^{(n)})-L_g(f_0)\}=L_g(W)$ has exactly the centered normal law $N(0,\sigma_g^2)$ by [F3]. On the event that both random scaled endpoints in step 2.1 lie within $\varepsilon$ of their limits, the event $L_g(f_0)\in C_{n,\alpha}$ is bounded between the corresponding deterministic normal-interval events with endpoints enlarged or contracted by $\varepsilon$. This sandwich uses no independence between the endpoints and the observation. The endpoint event has probability tending to one, and [F6] makes the normal mass of shrinking neighborhoods of the two endpoints tend to zero.

Letting $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ in the sandwich of step 3.1 gives limiting coverage $\Phi(z_{1-\alpha/2})-\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha$ by the definition of the normal quantiles and CDF in [F6].

For $v>0$ the law has density

If $Z_j$ are mutually independent with density $g$ and $\sum_{j\ge1}c_j^2=v<\infty$, and the finite sums $S_m=\sum_{j\le m}c_jZ_j$ converge in probability to a supplied real random variable $S$, then $S$ has law $N(0,v)$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: On the posterior event $\|f-f_0\|_2\le r_n\le\rho$, write $R(f)=\Psi(f)-\Psi(f_0)-L_g(f-f_0)$. The expansion gives $\sqrt n|R(f)|\le C\sqrt n r_n^2\to0$. Outside the event, posterior mass is $o_{P_{f_0}^{(n)}}(1)$ by assumption. Hence for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\Pi_n(\sqrt n|R(f)|>\varepsilon\mid X^{(n)})\to0$ in $P_{f_0}^{(n)}$-probability.

For posterior draws, $\sqrt n\{\Psi(f)-\theta_n^*\}=\sqrt n L_g(f-X^{(n)})+\sqrt nR(f)$. For $c_g=\max(1,\|L_g\|)$, composing a bounded $1$-Lipschitz scalar test with $L_g$ and dividing by $c_g$ gives an admissible bounded-Lipschitz test on $H(\delta)$. Thus the first term has bounded-Lipschitz distance to the pushforward limit at most $c_g$ times the distance in [F1]; by [F3] that limit is $N(0,\|g\|_2^2)$. For any bounded $1$-Lipschitz test function, replacing the first term by its sum with the remainder changes its posterior integral by at most $\varepsilon+2\Pi_n(\sqrt n|R(f)|>\varepsilon\mid X^{(n)})$. Step 1.1 and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ prove the asserted scalar BvM limit.

Apply [F4] to the centered and scaled posterior law in step 2.1. By [F6], its $\alpha/2$ and $1-\alpha/2$ quantiles converge in probability to $\|g\|_2z_{\alpha/2}$ and $\|g\|_2z_{1-\alpha/2}$. Translating and rescaling these quantiles gives the equal-tailed posterior interval for $\Psi(f)$; its credibility follows from [F5].

Under the true experiment, $\sqrt n\{\theta_n^*-\Psi(f_0)\}=L_g(W)$ has exactly the law $N(0,\|g\|_2^2)$ by [F3]. The random centered interval endpoints in step 3.1 converge in probability to the corresponding normal quantiles. For any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, on the event that both endpoints are within $\varepsilon$ of their limits, coverage is bounded by deterministic normal-interval probabilities with endpoints enlarged or contracted by $\varepsilon$. This argument requires no independence between the endpoints and $L_g(W)$. By [F6], the mass of shrinking endpoint neighborhoods vanishes; letting $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives coverage $1-\alpha$.

thm-nonlinear-functional-bvm-and-credibl.claim:
Use the white-noise experiment, product prior, and supplied posterior kernel of [[thm-weak-nonparametric-bernstein-von-mises-for-product-priors]], with all its stated basis, coefficient-density, truth, and countable-choice hypotheses. Let $\Psi:L^2([0,1])\to\mathbb R$ be Borel measurable. Suppose $f_0\in L^2$, and for some $g\in H^s_2$, $s>1/2$, $g\ne0$, $C<\infty$, and $\rho>0$,
$$|\Psi(f_0+h)-\Psi(f_0)-\langle h,g\rangle_{L^2}|\le C\|h\|_2^2\quad\text{whenever }\|h\|_2\le\rho.$$
Assume the posterior contracts in $L^2$ at a deterministic radius $r_n=o(n^{-1/2})$, meaning $\Pi_n(\|f-f_0\|_2>r_n\mid X^{(n)})=o_{P_{f_0}^{(n)}}(1)$. Define the efficient center
$$\theta_n^*:=\Psi(f_0)+L_g(X^{(n)}-f_0),$$
where the last pairing is the continuous $H(\delta)$ extension from [[lem-smooth-functional-extends-to-negative-sobolev-space]]. Then the posterior law of $\sqrt n\{\Psi(f)-\theta_n^*\}$ converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance to $N(0,\|g\|_2^2)$ in $P_{f_0}^{(n)}$-probability. The equal-tailed posterior interval for $\Psi(f)$ at level $1-\alpha$ is credible and has frequentist coverage tending to $1-\alpha$.

The radius assumption is the stronger convention required by this plan. It implies the source's squared-radius condition: with $s_n=r_n^2$, one has $s_n=o(n^{-1/2})$ and posterior mass inside $\|f-f_0\|_2^2\le s_n$ tends to one.
