def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noi.claim:
Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

lem-bounded-lipschitz-metric-characteriz.claim:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(S,d)$ be a Polish space, and let $\mu_n,\mu$ be Borel probability measures on $S$. Define

$$\beta_{BL}(\nu,\rho):=\sup\left\{\left|\int g\,d\nu-\int g\,d\rho\right|:g:S\to\mathbb R,\ \|g\|_\infty\le1,\ \operatorname{Lip}_d(g)\le1\right\},$$

where $\operatorname{Lip}_d(g):=\sup_{x\ne y}|g(x)-g(y)|/d(x,y)$, with value $0$ when $S$ has at most one point. Then

$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta_{BL}(\mu_n,\mu)\longrightarrow0,$$

where $\Rightarrow$ is weak convergence of Borel probabilities ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]). The implication from bounded-Lipschitz convergence to weak convergence is choice-free; the reverse implication below uses AC through Prokhorov's theorem.

citations.quote: For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.
Assume AC. A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a Polish space S is tight if and only if it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

u,ho)=0$, fix a nonempty closed $F$ and put $g_m=(1-md(\cdot,F))_+$. The function $g_m/m$ is an admissible test, so $\int g_m\,d
u=\int g_m\,dho$. By [F4], these integrals decrease to $
u(F)$ and $ho(F)$, respectively. The two probabilities therefore agree on every closed set, including the empty set. Closed sets form a pi-system generating the Borel sigma-algebra, and both total masses are one, so [F6] gives $
u=ho$. Thus $ eta_{BL}$ is a metric; this argument uses no choice.

Assume $\beta_{BL}(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$, and fix a nonempty closed set $F\subseteq S$. For every integer $m\ge1$, the function $g_m(x)=(1-md(x,F))_+$ satisfies $0\le g_m\le1$ and $\operatorname{Lip}_d(g_m)\le m$. Hence $g_m/m$ is admissible in the definition of $\beta_{BL}$, so $\int g_m\,d\mu_n\to\int g_m\,d\mu$. Since $1_F\le g_m$, it follows that $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\int g_m\,d\mu$ for every $m$.

Now assume $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$, and put $\mathcal A=\{\mu\}\cup\{\mu_n:n\ge1\}$. Any sequence chosen from $\mathcal A$ either has a member repeated infinitely often, yielding a constant convergent subsequence, or has a subsequence of the form $(\mu_{n_j})$ with $n_j\to\infty$, which converges weakly to $\mu$. Therefore $\mathcal A$ is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

The functions $g_m$ decrease pointwise to $1_F$ and are bounded by the integrable constant function $1$ under the probability $\mu$. By [F4], $\int g_m\,d\mu\to\mu(F)$, so the closed-set bound holds; it is trivial for $F=\varnothing$. The Portmanteau theorem [F2] gives weak convergence in the sense of [F1].

By [F5], $S$ is Polish; therefore [F3] applies under [A1] and $\mathcal A$ is tight. Thus for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq S$ such that $\sup_{\nu\in\mathcal A}\nu(K^c)<\varepsilon$.

Fix $\eta>0$. Compactness gives a finite $\eta/8$-net $x_1,\dots,x_q$ of $K$. Quantize each value $g(x_i)\in[-1,1]$ into finitely many bins of width at most $\eta/2$. There are finitely many resulting value patterns for the bounded 1-Lipschitz test class; choose one representative $h_r$ from each nonempty pattern. If $g$ and $h_r$ share a pattern, then for $x\in K$ a net point $x_i$ gives $|g(x)-h_r(x)|\le2d(x,x_i)+|g(x_i)-h_r(x_i)|<\eta$.

For any admissible $g$, choose the representative $h_r$ from its pattern. The integral difference is bounded by $\left|\int g\,d\mu_n-\int g\,d\mu\right|\le\max_r\left|\int h_r\,d\mu_n-\int h_r\,d\mu\right|+2\eta+2\mu_n(K^c)+2\mu(K^c).$ The maximum tends to zero by [F1], because there are finitely many bounded continuous representatives, and the last two terms are at most $4\varepsilon$ by step 2.2. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

derivations.claim:
The posterior draw $f$ and center $T_n$ are $L^2$-valued, so [F2] embeds $\sqrt n(f-T_n)$ in $M_0(w)$; [F1] supplies its norm. For an $L$-Lipschitz map $T$ between metric spaces and any admissible bounded 1-Lipschitz test $h$ on its target, $h\circ T/\max(1,L)$ is an admissible test on its domain. Therefore
$$\beta_{BL}(T_\#\nu,T_\#\rho)\le\max(1,L)\beta_{BL}(\nu,\rho).$$
By [F3], $J$ is linear and Lipschitz with a finite constant $L_J$. The bound applied pointwise to the data-indexed laws in [A1] gives $\beta_{BL}(J_\#Q_n,J_\#G_{P_0})\to0$ in probability. Moreover, if $\ell:C([0,1])\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and linear, then $\ell\circ J$ is continuous and linear on $M_0(w)$. The centered Gaussian premise on $G_{P_0}$ says exactly that this scalar pushforward is centered normal, allowing zero variance. Thus $J_\#G_{P_0}$ is a centered Gaussian Borel law. In particular, for any finite $t_1,\ldots,t_m$ and real $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, the functional $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iJx(t_i)$ is continuous and linear, so the evaluation vector $(JG_{P_0}(t_i))_{i=1}^m$ is jointly centered Gaussian. This uses only the scalar Gaussian pushforward meaning of the premise, without characteristic-function uniqueness or a Gaussian existence theorem. To identify its covariance, let $p_J1_{[0,s]}$ be the finite wavelet projection of the indicator. The finite Gaussian coefficient covariance gives
$$\operatorname{Cov}(J(P_JG_{P_0})(s),J(P_JG_{P_0})(t))=P_0[(p_J1_{[0,s]}-P_0p_J1_{[0,s]})(p_J1_{[0,t]}-P_0p_J1_{[0,t]})].$$
By [F11], $p_J1_{[0,s]}\to1_{[0,s]}$ in Lebesgue $L^2$; since $f_0\le B$, this is also convergence in $L^2(P_0)$. The variance of a difference of two finite projected Gaussian evaluations is the $P_0$-variance of the corresponding difference of projected indicators, so it tends to zero; hence those evaluations are Cauchy in $L^2$. They also converge almost surely to $JG_{P_0}(s)$ because $P_JG_{P_0}\to G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$ and $J$ is continuous. The almost-sure and in-probability limits coincide: for any $\varepsilon>0$, the probability that they differ by more than $\varepsilon$ is bounded by the two probabilities that each sequence differs from its limit by more than $\varepsilon/2$, both tending to zero. If $U_J,V_J$ are the projected evaluations and $U,V$ their $L^2$ limits, [F12] gives
$$|\mathbb E[U_JV_J]-\mathbb E[UV]|\le\|U_J-U\|_2\|V_J\|_2+\|U\|_2\|V_J-V\|_2\longrightarrow0;$$
the norms $\|V_J\|_2$ are bounded because $V_J\to V$ in $L^2$, and the means converge to zero as well. Thus the finite covariance passes to the limit. The resulting covariance is $P_0[(1_{[0,s]}-F_0(s))(1_{[0,t]}-F_0(t))]=F_0(s\wedge t)-F_0(s)F_0(t)$, the defining covariance of the $P_0$-Brownian bridge.

The norm maps $x\mapsto\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $F\mapsto\|F\|_\infty$ are 1-Lipschitz by the reverse triangle inequality. Applying the pushforward bound of step 1.1 first to the $M(w)$ norm and then to the supremum norm after $J$ gives bounded-Lipschitz convergence in probability of both posterior norm laws to their corresponding limit norm laws. Their CDFs satisfy [A3], so [F6] gives $R_n^M\to q_M$ and $R_n^C\to q_C$ in probability. For the projected empirical center $T_n=P_n(L_n)$, [F9] verifies [A2] under the smoothness and cutoff assumptions in [F9].

The posterior pushforward under either norm is a probability kernel on $[0,\infty)$. By [F5], the two lower quantiles are measurable and their posterior CDFs at those radii are at least $1-\alpha$. Since the centers and norms are measurable, the membership graphs of $C_n^M$ and $C_n^C$ are measurable. Thus both sets are credible by [F7].

By [A2] and [F4], $\sqrt n(T_n-f_0)\Rightarrow G_{P_0}$ and its primitive converges weakly to $B_{P_0}$. The frequentist error uses the negative center difference, but $\|f_0-T_n\|_{M(w)}=\|T_n-f_0\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|J(f_0-T_n)\|_\infty=\|J(T_n-f_0)\|_\infty$ because $J$ is linear. Thus each scaled frequentist error norm converges to the corresponding limit norm in [A3]. On the event that the random radius is within $\varepsilon$ of its deterministic limit from step 1.2, coverage is bounded above and below by probabilities for the frequentist norm with fixed thresholds expanded or contracted by $\varepsilon$. [F8] gives convergence of those fixed-threshold probabilities because [A3] makes their boundary probabilities zero. Sending $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using the CDF value $1-\alpha$ at its quantile from [A3] yields $1-\alpha$ for both coverage probabilities. This comparison does not require independence between the data-dependent posterior radii and the frequentist center.

thm-cdf-and-multiscale-credible-band-cal.claim:
Let $P_0$ have a density $f_0$ on $[0,1]$ bounded above and bounded away from zero, and put $F_0(t)=\int_0^t f_0(x)dx$. Use the wavelet basis and $M_0(w)$ of [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and assume the wavelet conditions and summability condition $\sum_lw_l2^{-l/2}<\infty$ of [[lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs]]. Let $T_n$ be a measurable $L^2$-valued center, let $\Pi_n$ be a posterior kernel supported on $L^2$ densities, and define $Q_n$ to be the conditional law on $M_0(w)$ of $\sqrt n(f-T_n)$ under $f\sim\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X^n)$.

Assume under $P_0^n$ that (i) $Q_n$ converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance in probability to the centered Gaussian bridge coefficient law $G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$, whose finite coefficient covariances are $P_0[(h-P_0h)(g-P_0g)]$, and (ii) $\sqrt n(T_n-f_0)\Rightarrow G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$. For $u=1-\alpha$, let $q_M$ and $q_C$ be the lower $u$-quantiles of $\|G_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|JG_{P_0}\|_\infty$. Assume both CDFs are continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on open neighborhoods of their respective quantiles, and that $q_M,q_C>0$. These local quantile conditions allow the CDFs to be constant on the negative half-line. In the projected empirical-center case $T_n=P_n(L_n)$, [[thm-projected-empirical-process-clt-in-m0w]] supplies premise (ii) under its stated smoothness and cutoff conditions. For the source-specific type-S and type-H priors, the posterior BvM premise (i) is established in [[thm-type-s-density-weak-bvm-on-m0w]] and [[thm-type-h-histogram-posterior-weak-bvm-in-m0w]], respectively.

For a posterior draw $f$, write $F_f=Jf$ and $F_{T_n}=JT_n$, where $J$ is the primitive map of [[lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs]]. Then the posterior law of $\sqrt n(F_f-F_{T_n})$ converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance on $C([0,1])$ to the $P_0$-Brownian bridge $B_{P_0}(t)$, with covariance $F_0(s\wedge t)-F_0(s)F_0(t)$.

For $0<\alpha<1$, let $R_n^M$ and $R_n^C$ be the posterior lower $1-\alpha$ quantiles of $\|\sqrt n(f-T_n)\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|\sqrt n(F_f-F_{T_n})\|_\infty$, respectively. The corresponding posterior balls
$$C_n^M=\{f:\|f-T_n\|_{M(w)}\le R_n^M/\sqrt n\},\qquad C_n^C=\{F:\|F-F_{T_n}\|_\infty\le R_n^C/\sqrt n\}$$
are measurable credible sets of posterior mass at least $1-\alpha$. Their frequentist coverage tends to $1-\alpha$, and the scaled radii converge to the respective $1-\alpha$ quantiles of $\|G_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|B_{P_0}\|_\infty$.

lem-density-bridge-norm-cdfs-are-continu.claim:
Assume AC. Let $P_0$ have density $0<\rho\le f_0\le D<\infty$ on $[0,1]$, and put $F_0(t)=\int_0^t f_0$. Use a complete real orthonormal wavelet basis, allowing the Haar basis with its finite scaling coordinate, and admissible weights $w$ as in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]]. Assume the wavelet geometry and summability conditions of [[lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs]], and write $J:M_0(w)\to C([0,1])$ for its primitive map. Let $G$ be the Borel centered Gaussian bridge random element of [[lem-density-gaussian-bridge-is-borel-on-m0w]], with coefficient covariance
$$\operatorname{Cov}(G_{lk},G_{l'k'})=P_0[(\psi_{lk}-P_0\psi_{lk})(\psi_{l'k'}-P_0\psi_{l'k'})].$$
Then the distribution functions of $\|G\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|JG\|_\infty$ are continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$. Both assign probability zero to $0$, and take values strictly between $0$ and $1$ at every positive argument. Consequently, for every $u\in(0,1)$, each has a unique positive finite lower $u$-quantile $q$, with CDF value $u$, and is strictly increasing on an open neighborhood of $q$.

citations.quote: For every weight sequence in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space. If $P_J$ retains exactly the coefficients at levels $l\le J$, then $\|P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\le\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$ for each $x\in M_0(w)$. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a compactly supported wavelet basis of [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The Haar basis with its finite scaling coordinate, as specified in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], is also allowed. Assume each level-$l$ wavelet for $l\ge l_0$ has zero integral, uniformly bounded overlap, support length at most $C_0 2^{-l}$, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. $$S_w:=\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}<\infty.$$
For $x\in M_0(w)$ define
$$Jx(t):=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle 1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle_{L^2},\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$
Then this series converges absolutely and uniformly in $t$, $Jx\in C([0,1])$, and $\|Jx-Jy\|_\infty\le C S_w\|x-y\|_{M(w)}$ after adding the finite coarsest-level constant to $C S_w$. If $x$ is the coefficient sequence of $f\in L^2$, then $Jx(t)=\int_0^t f(u)\,du$.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. Assume AC. Let $P_0$ have density $0\le f_0\le D<\infty$ on $[0,1]$, and let $(\psi_{lk})$ be an orthonormal wavelet system with at most $C2^l$ coordinates per level, including finitely many coarsest scaling coordinates. The Haar system is allowed. For every admissible $w$, there exists a Borel centered Gaussian random element $G_{P_0}$ of $M_0(w)$ with coefficient covariance
$$K((l,k),(l',k'))=P_0[(\psi_{lk}-P_0\psi_{lk})(\psi_{l'k'}-P_0\psi_{l'k'})].$$
Its Borel law is uniquely determined by these finite-coordinate Gaussian laws.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Two real Gaussian processes on the same index set
that have the same mean function and covariance function have identical
finite-dimensional distributions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The canonical centered Gaussian coordinate process
with covariance $E[X_sX_t]=\min(s,t)$ has a continuous modification $B$, and
$B$ is a standard Brownian motion. In particular, standard Brownian motion
exists.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion and, for
$0\le t\le1$, define

$$\beta_t=B_t-tB_1.$$

Then $\beta$ is a centered Gaussian process with one almost-surely continuous
path event,

$$\operatorname{Cov}(\beta_s,\beta_t)=\min(s,t)-st\qquad(0\le s,t\le1),$$

and $\beta_0=0$ almost surely while $\beta_1=0$ identically. This is the
standard Brownian bridge from $0$ to $0$ over $[0,1]$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion
[[def-brownian-motion]]. All path operations below use a fixed
everywhere-continuous, zero-start representative: choose a measurable
probability-one event on which the paths are continuous and $B_0=0$, and
replace $B$ by the zero path off this event, as in
[[def-wiener-measure-on-continuous-path-space]]. Retain the notation $B$ for
this representative and use its own raw natural filtration and usual
augmentation. This preserves every finite-dimensional law; all maxima and
hitting times below refer to this representative, without transferring
stopping times between the raw filtrations of different versions.
Let $a>0$ and $T>0$, and put
$$M_T:=\sup_{0\le s\le T}B_s,\qquad \tau_a:=\inf\{s\ge0:B_s=a\} .$$
Then:

1. The path reflected at $\tau_a$ has Wiener law: for each $T>0$ the process
   $(B_u)_{0\le u\le T}$ and its reflection $\widetilde B_u:=B_u$ for
   $u\le\tau_a\wedge T$, $\widetilde B_u:=2a-B_u$ for
   $\tau_a\wedge T<u\le T$, have the same law on the cylinder sigma-algebra
   $\sigma(\pi_u:u\in[0,T])$ of $\mathbb R^{[0,T]}$.
2. For every $b\le a$,
   $$P(M_T\ge a,\ B_T\le b)=P(B_T\ge2a-b),$$
   and in particular $P(M_T\ge a)=2P(B_T\ge a)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(U,V)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal real

$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The
covariance matrix may be singular.

[[def-brownian-motion]]. All path operations below use a fixed
everywhere-continuous, zero-start representative: choose a measurable
probability-one event on which the paths are continuous and $B_0=0$, and

$$M_T:=\sup_{0\le s\le T}B_s,\qquad \tau_a:=\inf\{s\ge0:B_s=a\} .$$
Then:

1. The path reflected at $\tau_a$ has Wiener law: for each $T>0$ the process
   $(B_u)_{0\le u\le T}$ and its reflection $\widetilde B_u:=B_u$ for
   $u\le\tau_a\wedge T$, $\widetilde B_u:=2a-B_u$ for
   $\tau_a\wedge T<u\le T$, have the same law on the cylinder sigma-algebra

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: In either $E=M_0(w)$ or $E=C([0,1])$, the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by countably many continuous linear coordinates: the wavelet coordinates in the first case, and evaluations at rational times in the second. Indeed, the norm distance to a fixed point is their countable supremum, with the weights included in the first case; in the second case continuity makes the rational supremum equal the full supremum. Separability then gives a countable base of coordinate-measurable balls. Separability of $M_0(w)$ is [F1]; rational polygonal functions give a countable dense family in $C([0,1])$ by uniform continuity and finite rational approximation. Thus finite-coordinate laws determine Borel laws by [F4]. If $X$ is any centered Borel Gaussian random element in either space and $X'$ an independent copy, [F3] gives $-X\overset d=X$ and $X+X'\overset d=\sqrt2X$: every finite coordinate vector on either side is centered Gaussian with the same covariance.

For the law $\mu$ of such an $X$, let $S$ be its support, the set of points whose every open neighborhood has positive probability. Its complement is the union of all zero-mass balls in a countable base, hence has measure zero by [F5]; $S$ is closed and nonempty. Symmetry from step 1.1 gives $S=-S$. The support of $X+X'$ is $\overline{S+S}$: independent positive-mass balls around $s,t\in S$ give positive mass to every neighborhood of $s+t$, proving one inclusion; the other follows because $X,X'\in S$ almost surely, so their sum lies almost surely in the closed set $\overline{S+S}$. Scaling by $\sqrt2$ is a homeomorphism, so step 1.1 gives $\sqrt2S=\overline{S+S}$. Taking any $s\in S$ and $-s\in S$ shows $0\in\sqrt2S$, hence $0\in S$. Now $x+0\in\overline{S+S}=\sqrt2S$ gives $S\subseteq\sqrt2S$, while $x+x\in\sqrt2S$ gives $\sqrt2x\in S$ and hence $\sqrt2S\subseteq S$. Therefore $\sqrt2S=S$ and $\overline{S+S}=S$. The set $S$ is additive and symmetric, and division by $2$ follows by applying division by $\sqrt2$ twice. It is closed under dyadic rational scalars, and closure gives all real scalars. Thus $S$ is a closed linear subspace.

If $X$ has any nondegenerate scalar coordinate, then $P(X=0)=0$ and $S\ne\{0\}$. For every $r>0$, $0\in S$ gives $P(\|X\|<r)>0$. A nonzero $s\in S$ can be scaled to have norm greater than $r$, so some neighborhood of that scaled point lies in $\{\|X\|>r\}$ and has positive probability. Likewise, for $0<a<b$, scale $s$ to have norm $(a+b)/2$; a sufficiently small ball about it is contained in $\{a<\|X\|<b\}$ and has positive probability. Consequently its norm CDF is strictly between zero and one at every positive argument and strictly increasing there. This applies to $G$: any nonconstant wavelet has positive $P_0$-variance, because $f_0\ge\rho$ makes the $P_0$ and Lebesgue null sets identical and a nonconstant wavelet cannot equal a constant almost everywhere.

For each nonzero $x\in M_0(w)$, its norm is attained by some coordinate: if $r=\|x\|_{M(w)}>0$, the normalized level maxima are below $r/2$ after finitely many levels, and the maximum over the remaining finite set equals $r$. Enumerate all coordinates by $j$, and write $b_j>0$ for their norm weights: $b_j=w_l$ on detail level $l$, and $b_j=1$ for any additional Haar scaling coordinate. Hence, for $r>0$, $\{\|G\|_{M(w)}=r\}$ is contained in the countable union of events $\{|G_j|=rb_j\}$. Each has probability zero: a positive-variance normal has a density, and a zero-variance centered normal is zero whereas $rb_j>0$. By [F5] the union is null. At $r=0$, the nondegenerate coordinate from step 1.3 again gives probability zero; negative values are impossible. Absence of atoms and continuity of probability in [F5] show that this norm CDF is continuous on $\mathbb R$.

Write $Y=JG$. For every continuous real linear functional $L$ on $C([0,1])$, $L\circ J$ is continuous linear on $M_0(w)$, so $L(Y)$ is centered normal by [F3]; thus $Y$ is centered Gaussian. For $s\in[0,1]$, let $p_N1_{[0,s]}$ be the orthogonal wavelet projection through level $N$. Its Lebesgue $L^2$ limit is $1_{[0,s]}$ by [F2], and $f_0\le D$ gives the same convergence in $L^2(P_0)$. Put $U_N(s)=J(P_NG)(s)$. The coefficient covariance in [F3] gives $\operatorname{Cov}(U_N(s),U_M(t))=P_0[(p_N1_{[0,s]}-P_0p_N1_{[0,s]})(p_M1_{[0,t]}-P_0p_M1_{[0,t]})]$. In particular $U_N(s)$ is Cauchy in $L^2$, and it converges almost surely to $Y(s)$ by [F1]. Its $L^2$ limit therefore equals $Y(s)$ almost surely, since convergence in $L^2$ implies convergence in probability and two probability limits agree. The means are zero; applying [F6] to the product differences passes the covariances to the limit. Thus $Y$ is a centered continuous Gaussian process with covariance $F_0(s\wedge t)-F_0(s)F_0(t)$. The function $F_0$ is a continuous strictly increasing bijection of $[0,1]$ onto itself. By [F3], $Y$ and $t\mapsto\beta_{F_0(t)}$ from [F7] have the same finite Gaussian laws; step 1.1 then gives equality of their Borel laws on $C([0,1])$. In particular $\|Y\|_\infty\overset d=\|\beta\|_\infty$, and $Y$ has a nondegenerate evaluation coordinate, for example at any $s$ with $0<F_0(s)<1$. Step 1.3 therefore applies to its norm as well.

Put $Z=B_1$ and $M=\max_{0\le t\le1}\beta_t$. Every finite vector of bridge values is jointly Gaussian with $Z$ and has zero cross-covariance, because $\operatorname{Cov}(B_t-tB_1,B_1)=t-t=0$. By [F8] these finite vectors are independent of $Z$. The coordinate generation in step 1.1 and finite-measure uniqueness [F4], applied to rectangles and then the generated sigma-algebra, show that the entire bridge path, and hence $M$, is independent of $Z$. Write $\phi$ for the standard-normal density. For $c>\varepsilon>0$, [F9] implies that the measure $P(\max_{t\le1}B_t<c,Z\in dz)$ on $[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$ has density $\phi(z)-\phi(2c-z)$: subtract the reflected-event measure from the terminal normal measure; the reflected-event CDF in [F9] differentiates to $\phi(2c-z)$ for $z<c$. Thus
$$A_\varepsilon(c):=\frac{P(\max_{t\le1}B_t<c,|Z|\le\varepsilon)}{P(|Z|\le\varepsilon)}=\frac{\int_{-\varepsilon}^{\varepsilon}[\phi(z)-\phi(2c-z)]\,dz}{\int_{-\varepsilon}^{\varepsilon}\phi(z)\,dz}.$$
For fixed $a>0$, take $0<\varepsilon<a/3$. Since $\|B-\beta\|_\infty\le\varepsilon$ on $\{|Z|\le\varepsilon\}$, the inclusions with thresholds $a-\varepsilon$ and $a+\varepsilon$, together with independence, give $A_\varepsilon(a-\varepsilon)\le P(M<a)\le A_\varepsilon(a+\varepsilon)$. Continuity and positivity of $\phi$ show that both bounds tend to $1-\phi(2a)/\phi(0)=1-e^{-2a^2}$. Hence $P(M<a)=1-e^{-2a^2}$ for every $a>0$. By [F5], $P(M\le a)=\lim_{k\to\infty}P(M<a+1/k)=1-e^{-2a^2}$ for $a>0$, and $M\ge0$ together with the same formula as $a\downarrow0$ gives $P(M=0)=0$. Therefore $M$ is atomless.

By symmetry of the centered Gaussian bridge, $-\min_t\beta_t$ has the same atomless distribution as $M$. For $r\ge0$, continuity on a compact interval gives $\{\|\beta\|_\infty=r\}\subseteq\{M=r\}\cup\{-\min_t\beta_t=r\}$. Both events on the right are null by step 4.1 and symmetry; [F5] gives no atom at $r$. Negative norm values are impossible. By step 3.1, the CDF of $\|JG\|_\infty$ is therefore continuous on $\mathbb R$.

Both norm CDFs are continuous by steps 2.1 and 4.2, vanish at zero, and are strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$ with values strictly between zero and one by steps 1.3 and 3.1. They tend to one at infinity because both random norms are finite almost surely. For each $u\in(0,1)$, continuity therefore gives a positive finite point $q$ with CDF value $u$, strict increase gives its uniqueness, and monotonicity makes it the lower $u$-quantile. Any sufficiently small open interval around $q$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$, where strict increase holds. These are all the asserted quantile conditions.

lem-density-gaussian-bridge-is-borel-on-.claim:
Assume AC. Let $P_0$ have density $0\le f_0\le D<\infty$ on $[0,1]$, and let $(\psi_{lk})$ be an orthonormal wavelet system with at most $C2^l$ coordinates per level, including finitely many coarsest scaling coordinates. The Haar system is allowed. For every admissible $w$, there exists a Borel centered Gaussian random element $G_{P_0}$ of $M_0(w)$ with coefficient covariance
$$K((l,k),(l',k'))=P_0[(\psi_{lk}-P_0\psi_{lk})(\psi_{l'k'}-P_0\psi_{l'k'})].$$
Its Borel law is uniquely determined by these finite-coordinate Gaussian laws.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$
\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.
$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

For every weight sequence in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space. If $P_J$ retains exactly the coefficients at levels $l\le J$, then $\|P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\le\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$ for each $x\in M_0(w)$. Every square-summable coefficient sequence belongs to $M_0(w)$.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: The displayed kernel is symmetric and positive semidefinite because for any finite coefficients $a_j$, $\sum_{i,j}a_i a_jK(i,j)=P_0[\sum_j a_j(\psi_j-P_0\psi_j)]^2\ge0$. Thus [F1] constructs a centered jointly Gaussian coordinate sequence $Z$ with this covariance. Each coordinate variance is at most $P_0\psi_{lk}^2\le D$.

For a centered normal of variance $v\le D$, completing the square in its normal density gives $\mathbb E e^{tZ}=e^{vt^2/2}$; at $v=0$ the variable is zero almost surely. Exponential Markov with $t=u/D$ therefore gives $\Pr(|Z|>u)\le2e^{-u^2/(2D)}$ when $D>0$, as it is for a probability density. Consequently $\Pr\{\max_k|Z_{lk}|>R\sqrt{l+1}\}\le2C2^l e^{-R^2(l+1)/(2D)}$. Choose $R$ with $R^2/(2D)>2\log2$. The sum over $l$ is finite, and the union bound over $l\ge J$ tends to zero. The probability that infinitely many of these events occur is therefore zero, since that event is contained in every such tail union.

Almost surely the normalized maxima $\max_k|Z_{lk}|/w_l$ tend to zero, by step 1.2 and admissibility $w_l/\sqrt{l+1}\to\infty$; each of the finitely many remaining coordinates is finite. The event $E=\{Z\in M_0(w)\}$ is coordinate-measurable, since the little-o condition is expressed by countable unions and intersections of the inequalities $\max_k|Z_{lk}|/w_l\le1/q$. It has probability one. Define $G=Z$ on $E$ and $G=0$ otherwise. Its finite projections are measurable finite-dimensional random elements and converge everywhere in the separable Banach space [F2]. Hence $G$ is Borel measurable: for every closed set $F$, the measurable functions $d(P_JG,F)$ converge to $d(G,F)$; inverse images of closed sets are thus measurable, and closed sets generate the Borel sigma-algebra.

Let $L$ be any continuous real linear functional on $M_0(w)$. Then $L(P_JG)\to L(G)$ almost surely, and each approximant is centered normal with some variance $v_J$. These variances are bounded. Indeed, almost-sure convergence makes the laws tight: choose $M$ so that $\Pr\{\sup_J|L(P_JG)|>M\}<1/2$, using that the supremum is finite almost surely. If $v_J\to\infty$ on a subsequence, the normal density bound would give $\Pr(|L(P_JG)|\le M)\le2M/\sqrt{2\pi v_J}\to0$, a contradiction. Any convergent subsequence of $(v_J)$ with limit $v$ gives, by [F3] and [F5], $\mathbb E e^{itL(G)}=e^{-vt^2/2}$. Taking $t=1$ shows that all subsequential variance limits coincide. Thus $v_J\to v\ge0$, and [F3] identifies $L(G)$ as $N(0,v)$. Therefore $G$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element.

Its coordinate covariance and finite Gaussian laws are unchanged by the null-set modification in step 2.1. Finally the Borel sigma-algebra of $M_0(w)$ equals the sigma-algebra generated by its countably many coordinates: the norm is their countable weighted supremum, so all open balls about a countable dense set are coordinate-measurable, and these balls generate the topology. Thus two Borel laws with the same finite-coordinate laws agree, by uniqueness of the cylinder law in [F1] restricted to this measurable space. This proves existence and uniqueness of the stated bridge law.

lem-finite-dirichlet-gamma-representatio.claim:
Assume AC. Let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m>0$, $B=\sum_j\beta_j$, and let $Z_j$ be independent $\operatorname{Gamma}(\beta_j,1)$ variables. Put $S=\sum_j Z_j$. Then $\omega=(Z_j/S)_j$ is $\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m)$, and $S$ is $\operatorname{Gamma}(B,1)$, with mean $B$ and variance $B$. Each $Z_j$ has mean $\beta_j$, variance $\beta_j$, and moment-generating function $\mathbb E e^{uZ_j}=(1-u)^{-\beta_j}$ for every real $u<1$. For real $q_j$ satisfying $|q_j|\le b$, put $T(q)=\sum_jq_j(Z_j-\beta_j)$ and $V=\sum_j\beta_jq_j^2$. If $V>0$, then for $x>0$,
$$\Pr\{|T(q)|>x\}\le2\exp\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2(V+bx)}\right\}.$$
If $V=0$, $T(q)=0$ almost surely. Sums of disjoint groups of the $Z_j$ are independent Gamma variables with their respective summed shapes.

Assume Countable Choice. For shape $a>0$ and rate $b>0$, the **shape-rate Gamma distribution**
$\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b)$ is the probability measure on $(0,\infty)$ with
density
$$f_{a,b}(\lambda)=\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}$$
relative to Lebesgue measure. Its normalization is proved in
[[lem-gamma-density-normalization]]. The second argument is a rate, not a scale.

Assume Countable Choice. For $a,b>0$,
$$\int_{(0,\infty)}\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}x^{a-1}e^{-bx}\,d\lambda_1(x)=1.$$

Assume Countable Choice. For $k\ge2$ and $\alpha_j>0$, the **Dirichlet distribution**
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)$ is the probability law
on the open probability simplex with density
$$\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \prod_jp_j^{\alpha_j-1}$$
relative to $dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1}$, with $p_k=1-\sum_{j<k}p_j$. Its
normalization is [[thm-dirichlet-density-normalization]]. For $k=1$, define
the law to be the point mass at $p_1=1$. All coordinates of the parameter
vector must be strictly positive.

spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of

2. for measurable rectangles,

4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Assume AC and let $k\ge0$. Let $
u$ be a finite complex Borel measure on $\mathbb R^k$. Suppose there is $\delta>0$ such that $\int e^{\delta\|x\|_1}\,|
u|(dx)<\infty$. If the Laplace transform $L(z)=\int e^{z\cdot x}\,

derivations.claim: The product Gamma law exists by [F3]. In its density make the substitution $z_j=s\omega_j$, $\omega_m=1-\sum_{j<m}\omega_j$. Its Jacobian is $s^{m-1}$: factor $s$ from the proportion columns of the derivative matrix and add its first $m-1$ rows to the last; the remaining last row has first entry one and all other entries zero. The resulting density factors as $s^{B-1}e^{-s}/\Gamma(B)$ times the simplex density in [F2]. Integrating either normalized factor proves both distributional assertions. For $m=1$, $\omega_1=1$ directly.

Substituting $y=(1-u)z$ in the Euler Gamma density gives $\mathbb E e^{uZ_j}=(1-u)^{-\beta_j}$ for $u<1$. Its first two derivatives at zero yield mean $\beta_j$ and variance $\beta_j$; differentiation is justified by an exponential majorant with any fixed parameter in $(0,1)$. Independence makes the joint transform of disjoint group sums the product $\prod_h(1-u_h)^{-\sum_{j\in I_h}\beta_j}$, which is the transform of the corresponding product Gamma law. By [F5], these are the same laws. In particular $S$ has the asserted mean and variance, also following from step 1.1.

For $|\lambda|b<1$, independence and step 1.2 give $\log\mathbb E e^{\lambda T(q)}=\sum_j\beta_j[-\log(1-\lambda q_j)-\lambda q_j]\le\lambda^2 V/[2(1-|\lambda|b)]$. Indeed the convergent logarithm series gives $-\log(1-u)-u\le\sum_{r\ge2}|u|^r/r\le u^2/[2(1-|u|)]$ for $|u|<1$. If $V>0$, set $\lambda=x/(V+bx)$; exponential Markov then bounds the upper tail by $\exp[-x^2/(2(V+bx))]$. Apply the same calculation to $-q$ and sum the bounds. If $V=0$, positivity of all $\beta_j$ forces every $q_j=0$, so $T(q)=0$.

thm-type-h-histogram-posterior-weak-bvm-.claim:
Assume AC. Use the type-H prior of [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]], retaining its original conditions: $1/2<\alpha\le1$, $f_0\in C^\alpha([0,1])$, $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$, either original cutoff $L_n=j_n$ or $L_n=\ell_n$, and $c_1 2^{-L_na}\le a_{k,L_n}\le c_2$ for fixed positive $a,c_1,c_2$. Write $m_n=2^{L_n}$. In the Haar convention, the scaling function is $1$, the detail functions are
$$\psi_{lk}=2^{l/2}(\mathbf1_{I_{l+1,2k}}-\mathbf1_{I_{l+1,2k+1}}),\qquad l\ge0,\quad 0\le k<2^l,$$
and a histogram at resolution $L_n$ has only the scaling coordinate and levels $l<L_n$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID from $f_0$, let $N_{nk}=\sum_i\mathbf1_{I_{L_n,k}}(X_i)$, and define the empirical histogram
$$h_n(x)=m_n N_{nk}/n\quad\text{on }I_{L_n,k}.$$
Let $\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X^n)$ be the density posterior for the stated histogram prior. For every nondecreasing $w_l\ge1$ with $w_l/\sqrt{l+1}\to\infty$, its conditional law $Q_n$ of $\sqrt n(f-h_n)$ satisfies
$$\beta_{BL,M_0(w)}(Q_n,\mathcal L(G_{P_0}))\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0^n$-probability, where the Borel centered Gaussian bridge $G_{P_0}$ is supplied by [[lem-density-gaussian-bridge-is-borel-on-m0w]] and has covariance $P_0[(\psi-P_0\psi)(\psi'-P_0\psi')]$. Its scaling coordinate is zero. This proves the type-H source-specific posterior BvM with the empirical projection center; no additional contraction, bias, or Dirichlet-parameter condition is imposed.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

u(dx)$ is zero for every real $z$ in an open neighborhood of $0$, then $
u=0$.

Let $d,k,m\ge1$ be fixed. For each $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y_n\in\mathbb R^k$ be random vectors on one probability space; the probability space may vary with $n$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ be a random vector on any probability space, and let $c\in\mathbb R^k$ be constant. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n-c=o_P(1)$, then
$$ (X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c). $$
Consequently, for every continuous $h:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R^m$, $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$. No independence between $X_n$ and $Y_n$ is required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(S,d)$ be a Polish space, and let $\mu_n,\mu$ be Borel probability measures on $S$. Define

$$\beta_{BL}(\nu,\rho):=\sup\left\{\left|\int g\,d\nu-\int g\,d\rho\right|:g:S\to\mathbb R,\ \|g\|_\infty\le1,\ \operatorname{Lip}_d(g)\le1\right\},$$

where $\operatorname{Lip}_d(g):=\sup_{x\ne y}|g(x)-g(y)|/d(x,y)$, with value $0$ when $S$ has at most one point. Then

$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta_{BL}(\mu_n,\mu)\longrightarrow0,$$

where $\Rightarrow$ is weak convergence of Borel probabilities ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]). The implication from bounded-Lipschitz convergence to weak convergence is choice-free; the reverse implication below uses AC through Prokhorov's theorem.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.
Every finite type-S draw and every type-H draw in [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]] is a well-defined nonnegative $L^2([0,1])$ probability density.

Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The same coefficient-space definition applies to the Haar system used for type-H histograms: detail levels $l\ge0$ have $2^l$ coefficients, and the single scaling coefficient is an additional finite coarsest coordinate, included in the norm with weight $1$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

derivations.claim: Abbreviate $m=m_n$, $a_k=a_{k,L_n}$, $A=\sum_ka_k$, $\beta_k=N_{nk}+a_k$, and $B=n+A$. The original cutoff conditions and $\alpha>1/2$ give $m/\sqrt n\to0$ and $m\log n/n\to0$, and $A\le c_2m$. On the positive simplex, the full-data histogram likelihood is $m^n\prod_k\omega_k^{N_{nk}}$. Multiplication by the prior density yields a constant times $\prod_k\omega_k^{\beta_k-1}$, with every shape positive; its normalization is finite positive by [F2]. Therefore the full-data posterior is Dirichlet$(\beta_k)_k$, regardless of whether the actual sampling truth is itself a histogram. By [F1] realize it by $\omega_k=Z_k/S$. Write $R_n$ for the posterior mean histogram measure, identified with its density in coefficient differences, with cell masses $\beta_k/B$. For a cell-constant function $q$, set $T(q)=\sum_kq_k(Z_k-\beta_k)$. Direct subtraction gives $\sqrt n(\omega q-R_nq)=(\sqrt n/S)T(q-R_nq)$.

Fix constants $t>0$ and $C$ large enough that $c:=tC-D_0(e^t-1)>0$. Since $N_{nk}$ is Binomial$(n,p_k)$ with $p_k=P_0I_{L_n,k}\le D_0/m$, independence of the observations gives $\mathbb E e^{tN_{nk}}=(1+p_k(e^t-1))^n\le e^{nD_0(e^t-1)/m}$. Hence $E_n=\{\max_kN_{nk}\le Cn/m\}$ satisfies $P_0^n(E_n^c)\le m e^{-cn/m}\to0$, by exponential Markov and the union bound. On $E_n$, for all sufficiently large $n$, $\beta_k\le C'n/m$, $B\le2n$, and both the empirical histogram density and the mean histogram density are bounded by a fixed constant $C'$ independent of $n$.

On $E_n$, take any Haar detail $\psi=\psi_{lk}$ with $l<L_n$ and put $q=\psi-R_n\psi$. Then $|q|\le2\,2^{l/2}$ and $V=\sum_k\beta_kq_k^2=B\operatorname{Var}_{R_n}(\psi)\le B R_n\psi^2\le C'n$, using $\int\psi^2=1$ and the density bound. By [F1] and [F7], $\Pr(S<B/2\mid X^n)\le4/B$, because $\operatorname{Var}(S)=B$. On the complement, step 1.1 yields $|\sqrt n(\omega\psi-R_n\psi)|\le2|T(q)|/\sqrt n$. Thus, apart from the single event $\{S<B/2\}$, the conditional probability that this absolute coefficient exceeds $x$ is at most $2\exp\{-c_0x^2/(1+2^{l/2}x/\sqrt n)\}$ for a fixed $c_0>0$. The zero-variance case has no such failure event, by [F1].

Choose a fixed $K>0$ sufficiently large. Uniformly over $l<L_n$, $2^{l/2}K\sqrt{l+1}/\sqrt n\le K\sqrt{m(L_n+1)/n}\to0$. Summing the exponential bounds of step 2.1 over levels $J<l<L_n$ and their $2^l$ coefficients therefore gives, for all large $n$, $\Pi_n\{\max_{J<l<L_n,k}|\sqrt n(f-R_n)_{lk}|/\sqrt{l+1}>K\mid X^n\}\le4/B+\sum_{l>J}2^{l+1}e^{-c_1K^2(l+1)}$ on $E_n$, with fixed $c_1>0$. The probability $4/B$ is counted only once, since the same $S$ normalizes every coordinate. Choose $K$ with $c_1K^2>2\log2$; the displayed series tail then tends to zero with $J$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, admissibility gives $K\sqrt{l+1}\le\varepsilon w_l$ for all sufficiently large $l$. Both $f$ and $R_n$ are histograms, so all their detail coordinates at $l\ge L_n$ vanish. Consequently their conditional $M(w)$ tails vanish in the iterated limit of [F4], first $n\to\infty$, then $J\to\infty$, since $P_0^n(E_n^c)\to0$.

For a Haar detail $\psi=\psi_{lk}$, exact subtraction gives $\sqrt n(R_n\psi-P_n\psi)=\sqrt n[\sum_ka_k\psi_k-A P_n\psi]/B$. Haar cell values satisfy $m^{-1}\sum_k|\psi_k|=\int|\psi|=2^{-l/2}\le1$. Hence $|\sum_ka_k\psi_k|\le c_2m$, while on $E_n$, $|P_n\psi|\le C\int|\psi|\le C$. This bounds every such mean shift by $C''m/\sqrt n\to0$. The scaling-coordinate shift is exactly zero, and all coordinates at $l\ge L_n$ vanish for both centers. Since $w_l\ge1$, $\|\sqrt n(R_n-h_n)\|_{M(w)}\to0$ uniformly on $E_n$. In particular step 2.2 also supplies the required posterior tails about $h_n$.

Fix finitely many Haar coordinates. Choose a fixed coarse dyadic partition of $r$ cells on which all their functions are constant. For large $n$ its cells are unions of level-$L_n$ cells. By [F1], the corresponding grouped Gamma variables $Z_{nj}$ are independent Gamma$(b_{nj},1)$ with $b_{nj}=N_n(J_j)+\sum_{I_{L_n,k}\subset J_j}a_k$. Their summed shape is still $B$. Write $p_j=P_0(J_j)>0$. Each coarse count satisfies $\mathbb E[N_n(J_j)/n]=p_j$ and variance at most $1/(4n)$, by observation independence. Markov applied to squared deviations, together with $A/n\to0$, proves $b_{nj}/n\to p_j$ in $P_0^n$-probability simultaneously for the fixed finite partition.

Consider any deterministic data sequence along which $b_{nj}/n\to p_j$ for every $j$. Under its conditional Gamma product laws put $Y_{nj}=(Z_{nj}-b_{nj})/\sqrt n$. For every fixed $t\in\mathbb R^r$, [F1] and the logarithm series give $\log\mathbb E e^{t\cdot Y_n}=\sum_j b_{nj}[-\log(1-t_j/\sqrt n)-t_j/\sqrt n]\to\tfrac12\sum_jp_jt_j^2$. The remainder is $O(n^{-3/2}\sum_jb_{nj}|t_j|^3)=O(n^{-1/2})$. The means of $Y_n$ are zero and their total second moments are $B/n=O(1)$, so their laws are tight by the squared-norm Markov bound and compactness of finite-dimensional closed balls. By [F5], any subsequence has a further weak limit. For any fixed $t$, the same expansion at $2t$ uniformly bounds $\mathbb E e^{2t\cdot Y_n}$; hence $e^{t\cdot Y_n}$ is uniformly integrable. Truncation of this continuous exponential therefore passes its expectation through each weakly convergent subsequence. The limit law has transform $\exp(\tfrac12\sum_jp_jt_j^2)$ and an exponential moment on a neighborhood of zero: $e^{\delta\sum_j|y_j|}\le\sum_{\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^r}e^{\delta\epsilon\cdot y}$ and the corresponding transforms are finite. The independent centered normal vector with variances $p_j$ has this same transform, by completing the square in each normal density. Transform uniqueness [F5] identifies every subsequential limit, proving $Y_n\Rightarrow N_r(0,\operatorname{diag}(p))$.

Here $(S-B)/\sqrt n=\sum_jY_{nj}$, $S/n\to1$ in conditional probability by its variance $B/n^2\to0$ and mean $B/n\to1$. Exact algebra gives $\sqrt n(Z_{nj}/S-b_{nj}/B)=(n/S)[Y_{nj}-(b_{nj}/B)\sum_hY_{nh}]$. By [F6] and step 3.2, this vector converges to $(U_j-p_j\sum_hU_h)_j$, with $U_j$ independent $N(0,p_j)$. Its covariance is $\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^T$. Applying the fixed linear map from coarse-cell masses to the chosen Haar coordinates yields covariance exactly $P_0[(\psi-P_0\psi)(\psi'-P_0\psi')]$. Step 2.3 removes the mean shift from $R_n$ to $h_n$ on $E_n$. Thus along every deterministic data sequence with the ratios in step 3.1 converging and $E_n$ eventually occurring, the finite-coordinate posterior converges weakly, hence in BL by [F6], to the corresponding projection of [F3].

The preceding deterministic-sequence conclusion implies the finite-coordinate BL convergence in $P_0^n$-probability. To see this without a simultaneous conditional null-set assertion, if that convergence failed, there would be $\varepsilon,\eta>0$ and infinitely many $n$ with probability at least $\eta$ that the distance exceeds $\varepsilon$. Along a subsequence, step 3.1 and $P_0^n(E_n^c)\to0$ make the probability of a ratio error above $1/q$ or $E_n^c$ smaller than $\eta/2$ at its $q$th chosen index. Thus at each such index there exists data with distance above $\varepsilon$, ratio error below $1/q$, and $E_n$ true. AC selects a deterministic sequence of those data, contradicting step 3.3. This proves the asserted convergence in probability for each fixed finite projection.

The posterior histogram construction [F8] and its finite-dimensional simplex kernel make $Q_n$ a data-indexed Borel probability on $M_0(w)$: each draw and $h_n$ has only finitely many Haar coefficients, and its map from simplex coordinates is continuous. The target is the Borel bridge law [F3]. Step 3.4 supplies every fixed finite-projection BL limit, and steps 2.2–2.3 supply its posterior-tail condition. Apply [F4] to obtain the stated $M_0(w)$ BL convergence. Every original type-H assumption has been retained; in particular the lower parameter bound is compatible with, but is not needed beyond, positivity in this conjugate proof.

citations.quote:
Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

derivations.claim: The finite orthogonal projection has kernel $K_L(x,y)=\sum_k\phi_{Lk}(x)\phi_{Lk}(y)$. At each $x$ only a uniformly bounded number of terms are nonzero, and each has $\|\phi_{Lk}\|_1\le C2^{-L/2}$. Thus $\int|K_L(x,y)|dy\le\sum_{k:\phi_{Lk}(x)\ne0}|\phi_{Lk}(x)|\|\phi_{Lk}\|_1\le C'$. A nonzero term requires $x,y$ to lie in one scaling support, giving the support bound. Also $K_L(x,x)=\sum_k\phi_{Lk}(x)^2\le C'2^L$; Cauchy–Schwarz on the scaling coefficients gives the claimed $L^2$ to $L^\infty$ bound.
For $h\in V_L$, $P_Lh=h$. Therefore $P_L(ah)(x)-a(x)h(x)=\int K_L(x,y)(a(y)-a(x))h(y)dy$. Hölder continuity, the support bound, and the kernel integral bound give the asserted commutator estimate.

The levelwise tail satisfies $\|\sum_k\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle\psi_{lk}\|_\infty\le CC_g2^{-\alpha l}$. Summing its geometric series over $l>L$ proves uniform convergence and the claimed approximation rate. Its uniform limit agrees with its $L^2$ limit, hence with $g$ almost everywhere, and everywhere for continuous representatives.

For composition put $u_j=P_jg$ and $v_j=u_j-u_{j-1}$, with the first finite low block treated as $u_0$. Levelwise derivative bounds and overlap give $\|v_j^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_g2^{j(q-\alpha)}$ for $0\le q\le m$, and $\|u_j^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_g^\prime2^{jq}$ for $1\le q\le m$ by summing levels; also $\sup_j\|u_j\|_\infty<\infty$. The identity $e^{u_j}-e^{u_{j-1}}=v_j\int_0^1e^{u_{j-1}+tv_j}dt$ and repeated product and chain rules therefore give, writing $H_j=e^{u_j}-e^{u_{j-1}}$, $\|H_j\|_\infty\le C2^{-j\alpha}$ and $\|H_j^{(m)}\|_\infty\le C2^{j(m-\alpha)}$. Indeed a derivative of order $q$ of the exponential factor is a finite sum of products of derivatives of its exponent of total order $q$, bounded by $C2^{jq}$; pairing with the derivative of order $m-q$ of $v_j$ gives $C2^{j(m-\alpha)}$.

The telescoping series $e^g=e^{u_0}+\sum_{j\ge1}H_j$ converges uniformly. For a wavelet at level $l$, the terms with $j\ge l$ have coefficients bounded by $C2^{-l/2}\sum_{j\ge l}2^{-j\alpha}\le C2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$. For $j<l$, subtract the degree $m-1$ Taylor polynomial of $H_j$ about a point of the wavelet support; all its integrals vanish by the stated moments. The Taylor remainder gives $|\langle H_j,\psi_{lk}\rangle|\le C2^{-l(m+1/2)}2^{j(m-\alpha)}$. Sum the geometric series over $j<l$ to get the same $C2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$ bound. The fixed smooth $e^{u_0}$ has the stronger order $2^{-l(m+1/2)}$. This proves composition in the coefficient class directly, for every positive $\alpha$ including integers, without presuming a Hölder–wavelet equivalence.

For $0<\beta<\min(\alpha,1)$ the levelwise derivative and supremum bounds for $g$ are respectively at most $C2^{j(1-\beta)}$ and $C2^{-j\beta}$. Given distance $0<\delta<1$, choose $J$ with $2^{-J-1}<\delta\le2^{-J}$. The difference of the levels through $J$ is at most $C\delta\sum_{j\le J}2^{j(1-\beta)}\le C\delta^\beta$ by the derivative bound; the remaining difference is at most $C\sum_{j>J}2^{-j\beta}\le C\delta^\beta$. Thus $g$ is $\beta$-Hölder. The exponential has bounded derivative on the bounded range of $g$, so $e^g$ has the same Hölder bound.

lem-compact-wavelet-projection-kernel-an.claim:
Let $V_L$ be the span of wavelets through level $L$ in a compactly supported orthonormal multiresolution basis on $[0,1]$, either boundary corrected or periodized. Assume constants belong to $V_L$, its dimension $d_L\asymp2^L$, and its orthonormal scaling functions $\phi_{Lk}$ have supremum norm at most $C2^{L/2}$, support diameter at most $C2^{-L}$, and uniformly bounded overlap. Periodized supports and distances are interpreted on the circle. Assume also $\sum_k|\psi_{lk}(x)|\le C2^{l/2}$ and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C2^{-l/2}$. Let $P_L$ denote the orthogonal projection onto $V_L$.

Then $P_L$ has a kernel $K_L$ satisfying $\sup_x\int|K_L(x,y)|dy\le C'$ and $K_L(x,y)=0$ when $\operatorname{dist}(x,y)>C'2^{-L}$. If $a$ is $\beta$-Hölder for $0<\beta\le1$, then
$$\|P_L(ah)-ah\|_\infty\le C'\|a\|_{C^\beta}2^{-\beta L}\|h\|_\infty,\qquad h\in V_L.$$
For the composition assertion, assume additionally an integer $m>\alpha$ such that $\|\psi_{lk}^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_q2^{l(q+1/2)}$ for $0\le q\le m$, bounded overlap also for their derivatives, and vanishing moments through degree $m-1$ for the detail wavelets, including boundary wavelets; the finite low scaling functions are $C^m$. These are the usual sufficiently regular compact wavelet hypotheses. If a bounded function $g$ has coefficients bounded by $C_g2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, with $\alpha>0$, and its wavelet expansion represents $g$ in $L^2$, then $\|g-P_Lg\|_\infty\le C''C_g2^{-\alpha L}$, up to equality of the continuous representatives. Under these additional derivative and cancellation hypotheses, $e^g$ also has coefficients bounded by $C_g^\prime2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, including integer $\alpha$, and $g,e^g$ are $\beta$-Hölder for every $0<\beta<\min(\alpha,1)$. Moreover $\|h\|_\infty\le C''\sqrt{d_L}\|h\|_2$ for $h\in V_L$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

derivations.claim: Quotient out constants before using likelihood curvature. Constants belong to the fixed low scaling space. An orthogonal change within that finite space separates $T=\theta+c1$; integrate $c$ out of the prior and write $q_L$ for the resulting Lebesgue density on $E_L$. The likelihood depends only on $\theta$. In S1 its product density before integration obeys $p(\theta+u,c)/p(\theta,c)\in[e^{-B_L\|u\|_2},e^{B_L\|u\|_2}]$, where $B_L^2\le C\sum_{l\le L}2^l\sigma_l^{-2}\le Cd^{2\alpha+2}$. Integrating preserves both inequalities for $q_L$; it is positive, finite almost everywhere, and the log-Lipschitz inequality supplies its positive continuous finite version everywhere. In S2 the marginal is a nondegenerate Gaussian on $E_L$, with precision $Q_L$ equal to $\sigma_l^{-2}$ on high wavelets and a fixed positive definite low block; hence $\|Q_L\|\le Cd^{2r+1}$.

Let $f_*=e^{\theta_*}/\int e^{\theta_*}$. [F1] gives $\|f_*-f_0\|_\infty\le Cd^{-\alpha}$. For $\ell(\theta)=n(P_n\theta-\log\int e^\theta)$, the centered score at $\theta_*$ has expected squared Euclidean norm at most $Cnd$: sum the coordinate variances, each bounded by $D_0$ by orthonormality. The score's deterministic mean is the coefficient vector of $n(f_0-f_*)$, with norm at most $Cnd^{-\alpha}$. Consequently [F3] gives $\|\nabla\ell(\theta_*)\|_2=O_P(ne_n)$. On every ball $\|u\|_2\le Re_n$ with fixed $R$, [F1] and $\sqrt d e_n\to0$ make $f_{\theta_*+u}$ bounded uniformly above and away from zero. For $v\in E_L$, $\operatorname{Var}_f(v)=\inf_a\int(v-a)^2f$ lies between $c\|v\|_2^2$ and $C\|v\|_2^2$, using $\int v=0$. Thus $-\nabla^2\ell$ is between $cnI$ and $CnI$ on these balls. Convexity of $-\ell$ holds globally.

In S1, $B_L\le Cne_n$ by either cutoff. In S2 the Hölder coefficient bound gives $G_L^2:=\|Q_L\theta_*\|_2^2\le C[1+\sum_{l\le L}2^{l(4r+2-2\alpha)}]$, so $G_L\le Cne_n$, and $\|Q_L\|/n\to0$ because $r<\alpha$. The Gaussian log-density increment is exactly $-\langle Q_L\theta_*,u\rangle-\langle Q_Lu,u\rangle/2$. In particular its radial upper slope is at most $G_L$, and on the $e_n$ ball it is bounded below by $-G_Le_n-\|Q_L\|e_n^2/2$.

Fix a score event $\|\nabla\ell(\theta_*)\|_2\le Ane_n$. Put $r_0=Re_n$, with $R$ a large fixed constant. Taylor's formula on the $r_0$ ball bounds $\ell(\theta_*+r_0\omega)-\ell(\theta_*)$ above by $Ane_nr_0-cnr_0^2/2$ and its radial derivative above by $Ane_n-cnr_0$. Global convexity of $-\ell$ extends this derivative bound to every $r\ge r_0$. Add the prior bound $B_Lr$ in S1, or $G_Lr$ with its nonpositive quadratic term in S2. For $R$ large enough the log unnormalized posterior ratio $H(r\omega)$ relative to $\theta_*$ is at most $-c'nr_0r$ for all $r\ge r_0$. On $r\le e_n$, the lower Taylor bound and the prior lower bounds instead give $H\ge-C_Ane_n^2$.

Polar integration in dimension $m=d-1$ bounds the tail/normalizer ratio by $e^{C_Ane_n^2}m\int_R^\infty t^{m-1}e^{-c'nRe_n^2t}dt$. Here $ne_n^2\ge d>m$. Choose $R$ so large that $\log t\le c'Rt/4$ for $t\ge R$ and $C_A\le c'R^2/4$. The integral is then at most $[m/(c''nRe_n^2)]e^{-c''nR^2e_n^2}$ after decreasing $c''>0$, and tends to zero. The denominator used here is the integral on the $e_n$ ball, at least its volume times $e^{-C_Ane_n^2}$ times the positive unnormalized value at $\theta_*$. First increase $A$ to make its score event arbitrarily probable, then increase $R$. This proves tightness. For any $b_n\to\infty$, eventual containment of every fixed $Re_n$ ball in the $b_ne_n$ ball yields the stated equivalent formulation.

Every modeled density is everywhere positive. Its prior predictive product density is positive and integrates to one by [F2], so it is finite Lebesgue-almost everywhere on the sample cube. The law $P_0^n$ has a bounded Lebesgue density, hence the same exceptional set is $P_0^n$-null. This proves finite positive evidence on the asserted fibers independently of the score event.

Proof 2.2: polar integration is used only at sufficiently large n, when d-1>0; finite n do not affect contraction. Proof 3.1 treats evidence for every finite n.
Proof 1.1: Gaussian marginal low-block precision is positive definite on the quotient; the original likelihood-degenerate constant direction is removed rather than assigned false curvature.
